Training syllabus

15 phases · 28 modules

Every topic below is taught somewhere in this academy. Click a module to open it. The objective is not simply to teach an agent how to use Limo Anywhere — it is to develop an agent who understands the transportation business behind each transaction and can apply that knowledge accurately within the software while providing professional customer and operational support.

Phase 1 · Chauffeured transportation industry fundamentals

Industry & operational overview

≡ Syllabus · Phase 1 · Module 1
≈ 40 min
Section 01

The ground transportation industry

≈ 15 min
≡Definition

Ground transportation is pre-arranged, chauffeured car service: a customer books ahead, a licensed company sends a professional driver in a specific class of vehicle, and the price is agreed before the trip.

The company is called an operator. Limo Anywhere is the software an operator runs on. You will help operators use it.

»Example

"Pick me up at DFW at 11, take me to the Hilton, in an SUV." The operator quotes $165, sends Darrell in a Yukon, and bills the customer's company afterwards.

✓Key points
  • Not ride-hailing: no surge meter, price known up front
  • Booked in advance, often by an assistant for someone else
  • Who pays, who books and who rides can be three different people
  • Everything the software does hangs off one booked trip
1.1 Where this industry s…1.2 What operators actual…1.3 Black car and chauffe…1.4 Who is in the picture1.5 Who books, and what t…1.6 Life of a trip1.7 Reservation to billing1.8 The six operating fun…1.9 Corporate, retail and…1.10 What good looks like1.11 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 11

1.1 Where this industry sits

In plain words — "Ground transportation" covers a lot of businesses that have little to do with each other. Taxis, neighbourhood livery, black car, limousine and chauffeured service, shared-ride shuttles, charter buses and non-emergency medical transport all sit under the term. The operators you will support are the black car and limousine end of it.

What the customer is actually buying

The vehicle is the least of it. A prearranged, for-hire trip is sold on things the customer cannot see in advance and will only notice if they go wrong.

Reliability

The car is there, at the right place, at the right time, on a day the customer has planned around it.

Professional service

A chauffeur who knows the job: appearance, discretion, luggage, door service, and knowing when not to talk.

Accurate coordination

The flight, the terminal, the name on the board, the account reference, the second passenger nobody mentioned until yesterday.

Safety

Licensed, insured, inspected, and driven by someone who has been checked.

Discretion

Who travelled, where, and with whom is not discussed. This is why Module 4 is strict about what you may tell a caller.

Support when plans change

The part you are being hired for. Anyone can deliver a trip that goes to plan.

Why this matters to an agent

Every one of those six is delivered by a person rather than by the car — and on an overnight shift, several of them are delivered by you. A customer does not experience "the dispatch system". They experience whether someone knew what was happening and told them.

One trip, seven departments

A single reservation passes through reservations, dispatch, the chauffeur, customer care, affiliate relations, billing and fleet. Traffic, weather, a flight change, a wrong detail typed at booking, a vehicle fault or a last-minute request can disturb any of them. That is why operators run both software and experienced staff: the software holds the plan, and the staff handle the exceptions.

The plan

"What should happen?"

Reservations, rates, assignments and schedules. This is what the system is good at, and what most of this academy teaches you to operate.

The exception

"What actually happened?"

A delay, a diversion, a breakdown, a change of mind. No system resolves these on its own; they need judgement, and a person on the phone.

The record

"What did we do about it?"

Notes, statuses, documented calls. This is how the next shift, the dispatcher and accounting find out — and how a dispute gets settled.

Lesson 2 of 11

1.2 What operators actually sell

What operators actually sell

Point-to-point

Address to address at a fixed price. The bread and butter of retail and corporate work.

Airport arrivals & departures

Pickups tied to a flight number; the driver's spot time moves with the flight. Customers are, in Brandon's words, "insane" about airport pickups.

Hourly / as-directed

The customer buys the vehicle and driver for a block of hours; drop-off is optional. Billed per hour with minimums.

Charter, tours & shuttles

Minibuses and motor coaches, often priced per passenger or per hour with tiered rates.

Lesson 3 of 11

1.3 Black car and chauffeured service compared

In plain words — "Black car" and "limousine" get used interchangeably, but they usually describe two different operating models. Knowing which one a client runs tells you what they will care about, how quickly they expect you to act, and what a good decision looks like on their account.
AreaBlack car serviceLimousine & chauffeured service
Primary demandA mix of immediate, near-term and advance requests, often from corporate accounts.Mostly advance reservations tied to a confirmed pickup time and detailed service requirements.
Service modelEfficient point-to-point transportation, airport service, corporate travel.Premium, closely managed service for executives, events, hourly bookings, road shows and occasions.
Fleet structureOften relies heavily on independent operators who own or lease their own vehicles.May use company-owned vehicles, employee chauffeurs, independent operators, or a blend.
Vehicle expectationsLate-model black sedans and SUVs; standards vary by operator and market.Latest-model luxury sedans, SUVs, vans, stretch limousines, minibuses and specialty vehicles.
Driver presentationProfessional appearance and conduct, to company or corporate-account standards.Formal chauffeur standards: business attire, luggage assistance, door service, detailed trip preparation.
Dispatch priorityFast response, driver availability, proximity, account requirements.On-time performance, planned assignments, vehicle presentation, chauffeur preparation, active monitoring.
Pricing and paymentAccount rates, zone or flat rates, time and mileage, vouchers, direct billing or card.Base or transfer rates, hourly minimums, mileage, waiting time, garage time, gratuity, fees, account or card.
These are common practices, not legal definitions

Plenty of companies run both models, and many run them on one platform across several brands or legal entities — which is why a Limo Anywhere account can carry more than one company alias. Never assume from the company’s name which model you are working on; read the client’s SOP pack.

What the difference means on a shift

On a black car account

Expect more same-day and ASAP work, more decisions about who is nearest, and more pressure on speed of response. The dispatch question is usually "who can get there?"

On a chauffeured account

Expect the day to be planned well in advance, and the value to be in protecting that plan — spot times, vehicle presentation, the right chauffeur on the right client. The dispatch question is usually "will this still work?"

Lesson 4 of 11

1.4 Who is in the picture

Who is in the picture

Every trip has more people attached than the one in the back seat. Understanding these roles is the single most useful thing you can do before opening a reservation screen, because Limo Anywhere's account model is built directly on them.

Billing contact

"Who pays?"

The person or department responsible for the bill. Might be an individual, or "Accounts Payable" at a corporation. Has the card on file or the invoice terms.

Booking contact

"Who called?"

The executive assistant or travel coordinator who makes the booking on someone else's behalf. Gets the confirmation.

Passenger

"Who rides?"

The person in the car. Gets the driver-on-the-way text. Often the same human as the other two in retail; often three different people in corporate work.

Operator

The transportation company running the software — your customer. Owns the fleet, the drivers, the rates and the client relationships.

Affiliate

Another operator, usually in a different city. Work sent to them is a farm-out; work received from them is a farm-in. Networks like LA Net, GNet, GroundSpan and Ground Exchange connect them.

Agent

A booking agent or travel partner paid a commission (say 5%) on every trip they send. Tracked so they can be paid at settlement.

Lesson 5 of 11

1.5 Who books, and what they book

Most trips are not booked by the person riding in the car. Knowing who is on the phone tells you what they already know, what they need from you, and how much of their time you may take.

Where the work comes from

Corporate travel

Travel managers, executive assistants, office administrators. Volume, negotiated rates, direct billing, and a low tolerance for being asked things twice.

Hospitality & travel trade

Hotels, concierge desks, travel agencies, tour planners. Often booking for a guest they will never meet again, and passing on second-hand detail.

Meetings & events

Meeting planners, event companies and DMCs — destination management companies that coordinate transport, meetings, tours and events in a city.

Road shows & finance

Road show coordinators, investment firms, executive travel teams. Multi-stop days, tight timing, cars held for hours.

Aviation

Airlines, private aviation providers and airport service partners. Crew moves, FBO work, and disruption recovery.

Retail

Individuals booking an airport run, an hourly car or a special occasion. Fewer assumptions to rely on, so more explaining.

And the seventh source: other transportation companies

Affiliates exchange work in markets where they have no fleet of their own. That trip arrives as a farm-in and is a real booking with a real passenger — it simply came from a company rather than a customer. Module 22 covers both directions.

What they book

Trip typeWhat makes it distinctive
Airport transferTiming set by an aircraft rather than the customer. Module 8.
Point-to-pointOne pickup, one destination. The industry’s staple, often priced as a transfer at a fixed rate.
Hourly / as-directedThe vehicle and chauffeur are bought for a block of time; a destination is optional. Minimum hours apply.
Corporate meetingsShort hops between offices, often several in a day on one account.
Road showsA car held for a team across a packed day of meetings, frequently across cities.
Group movements & eventsMultiple vehicles and movements. Module 15.
Recurring / standing ordersThe same trip on a defined schedule. Built once, repeated — and therefore repeated wrongly if built wrongly.
ASAPA car as soon as one can get there. Module 13.

Lesson 7 of 11

1.7 Reservation to billing: the eight stages

In plain words — "Life of a trip" showed the statuses a trip moves through. This is the same journey seen from the office: eight stages, each owned by somebody, each capable of breaking the one after it. You will work in most of them.
1Reservation entryA customer or arranger gives the passenger, pickup, destination, date and time, flight, vehicle, payment and any special-service detail. Modules 4–7 and 12.
2Review and confirmationThe trip requirements, rate, account instructions, contact details and any operational notes are confirmed. This is the stage where a wrong detail is cheap to fix.
3Planning and assignmentDispatch schedules a suitable chauffeur and vehicle, or sends the trip to an approved affiliate. Advance work may be assigned days ahead; ASAP work is assigned on availability and proximity. Modules 16, 19, 22.
4Pre-trip monitoringOperations checks the chauffeur is available, prepared and progressing toward the pickup, and watches flight status, traffic and weather. Modules 17 and 18 — this is where the wake-up call lives.
5Passenger communicationConfirmations, chauffeur and vehicle details, arrival notices and updates. Some black car operations have an agent call the passenger with the car number and an ETA — the "knock-off" call. Module 17.
6Service deliveryThe chauffeur arrives, reports the required statuses, carries the passenger, and records waiting time, stops, tolls, parking and anything else billable. Module 19.
7Trip closeoutAfter drop-off the trip is closed and reviewed: actual times, charges, chauffeur or affiliate pay, documentation, account-specific rules. Modules 23 and 24.
8Billing and paymentAccounting finalises the rate, invoices the account or takes the payment, and resolves exceptions and supporting-document requests. Module 25.
Stages 2 and 4 are the cheap ones to get right

An error caught at confirmation costs a question. The same error caught at stage 6 costs a failed pickup, and at stage 8 costs an invoice dispute. Most of what this academy asks of you — read back, verify, check before you confirm, watch the board — is an attempt to move problems earlier in this list.

Lesson 8 of 11

1.8 The six operating functions

Six functions, in every operator of any size. In a small company one person may do four of them; in a large one each is a department. Your work touches all six, so it helps to know whose toes you are near.

Reservations

Capturing complete, accurate information. A wrong terminal, airline, phone number, pickup entrance, passenger name or service time creates an operational problem later, not now. Corporate accounts add billing references, passenger profiles, approval codes and account-specific instructions.

You work here constantly. Modules 4–7, 11–12.

Dispatch & quality control

Matching trips to qualified drivers and vehicles, watching status, reacting to delays, communicating changes. Black car operations often dispatch by zone or closest vehicle for immediate work; chauffeured operations plan ahead and use QC staff to watch on-time performance and readiness.

You assist here. Modules 16–19 — and Module 19 draws the line you must not cross.

Drivers & chauffeurs

Drivers may be employees, independent operators or affiliate chauffeurs, and which one changes scheduling, pay, vehicle ownership, insurance and how much direct control the company has. Expectations usually include appearance, safe driving, discretion, luggage assistance, clear communication and correct use of the driver app.

You communicate with them. Modules 17–19.

Fleet & vehicle management

Availability, licensing, insurance, inspections, cleaning, maintenance, fuel or charging, replacement planning — plus matching each reservation to the right vehicle type, passenger capacity, luggage capacity, accessibility need and account standard.

You depend on it. Module 3 and lesson 27.4.

Affiliate operations

Covering work outside the operating area, or when the fleet is committed. A trip sent away is a farm-out; one received is a farm-in. It runs on agreed rates, service standards, insurance documentation, communication procedures and timely confirmation of chauffeur and vehicle details.

You coordinate it. Module 22.

Accounting & driver pay

Reviewing completed trips, applying rates and fees, processing cards or direct billing, preparing invoices, managing adjustments, and calculating chauffeur or affiliate pay. Charges commonly include a base or transfer rate, hourly minimum, mileage, waiting time, garage time, tolls, parking, gratuity and administrative or surface transportation charges.

You support it. Modules 23–25.

Technology does not replace any of them

A modern platform runs the whole lifecycle: reservations, customer profiles, pricing, dispatch, GPS, driver apps, automated notifications, flight tracking, payment processing, invoicing, affiliate exchange, reporting and audit history. That is what Limo Anywhere is, and Phase 4 onward teaches it.

But automation is only as good as the data under it

A dispatcher still needs to understand geography, traffic, what a vehicle can actually do, chauffeur schedules, account rules and the consequences of moving a trip. Flight tracking only helps if somebody typed the right flight number. Rates only calculate if somebody set them up. Every automatic behaviour in this academy rests on a field an agent filled in — which is the real reason accuracy is laboured so heavily here.

Lesson 9 of 11

1.9 Corporate, retail and after-hours

In plain words — The same trip behaves differently depending on who is buying it. A retail customer pays with a card and disappears. A corporate customer is booked by an assistant, invoiced monthly, and will be back next Tuesday. Knowing which one you are talking to changes what you ask, what you may promise, and how carefully you record it.

Retail

An individual booking for themselves or their family — a wedding, a night out, an airport run. Pays by card at the time of booking. Usually books once. Price sensitive, and often unfamiliar with how chauffeured service works, so they need more explanation than a corporate caller.

Corporate

A company with an account. Rides are booked by assistants and travel arrangers, charged to a cost centre, and invoiced on terms. Rates are often negotiated and lower than retail. Service expectations are higher and failures are remembered, because the same account books every week.

The travel arranger

Most corporate work reaches you through a travel arranger — an executive assistant, an office manager, a travel desk, or a third-party travel management company. They are not riding. They may be booking for several different passengers in one call, and they will judge you on how little of their time you take.

They know the routine

Do not explain what a meet & greet is to someone who books forty a month. Confirm, do not educate.

They rarely know the flight

Arrangers often book before travel is finalised. Take the booking, flag the missing flight, and chase it rather than refusing.

They are the one you update

The passenger gets the driver text. The arranger gets the confirmation, the change notice and the problem call.

After hours is a different job

Most of a GroundOps agent's shifts are outside the client's own office hours. That is the point of the service: when something goes wrong at 02:40, there is a person awake. It also means you are frequently the only one on, which changes the calculus of every decision.

During client office hoursAfter hours
Someone in the client's office can approve an exception in a minute.Approval may take 20 minutes or may not come at all until morning.
Escalation is a transfer.Escalation is a phone call to a named person who is asleep. The bar is higher — and when it is met, you call anyway.
Most calls are bookings.Most calls are exceptions: a delayed flight, a driver who has not arrived, a passenger who cannot find their car.
Documentation is helpful.Documentation is the only record anyone will have in the morning. If it is not written down, it did not happen.
The after-hours rule

If a passenger is stranded, a vehicle has broken down, or a ride is about to fail, you escalate while you keep working the problem — not after you have exhausted every option yourself. Waking the right person at 03:00 over a genuine service failure is correct. Discovering it at 08:00 is not.

Lesson 10 of 11

1.10 What good looks like

In plain words — Operators in this industry compete on consistency rather than on price or on having nicer cars. Nearly everything measured is something an agent can affect on a single shift.

What gets measured

MeasureWhere you affect it
On-time arrival and completed-trip performanceSpotting a late run before the passenger does, and escalating early. Modules 17, 20.
Reservation accuracy and response timeThe fifteen fields, the read-back, and answering email inside the client’s target. Modules 5, 7.
Chauffeur acceptance, availability and status complianceWatching for trips still unaccepted, and wake-up calls made on time. Modules 18, 19.
Vehicle quality and correct vehicle assignmentBooking the class that actually fits the passengers and the luggage. Module 3.
Passenger communication and complaint resolutionCalling before they call you; recording and routing complaints properly. Modules 6, 17.
Handling flight, traffic, weather and last-minute changesThe impact check, and knowing what you may and may not agree to. Modules 8, 13.
Accurate closeout, billing, chauffeur pay and affiliate reconciliationThe twelve checks and an honest settlement pass. Modules 23–25.
Why handoffs and records keep coming up

Because every reservation crosses several departments, a company can only investigate a problem if the trail exists. Audit history, trip notes, recorded communications and exception reports are what management uses to work out what happened and stop it happening again. An undocumented save is invisible to all of it — which is why Module 26 exists.

What the industry is up against

Competition

Traditional operators, app-based transportation and local providers, all reachable in one tap.

People

Recruiting, retaining and training drivers, and finding independent operators when demand spikes.

Costs

Vehicles, insurance, labour, fuel, technology and regulation, all rising.

Demand swings

Business travel, the economy, major events, weather and season. A quiet Tuesday and a marathon Sunday are different businesses.

Expectations

Immediate confirmations, live updates, mobile payment and transparency — benchmarked against apps, not against limousine companies.

The balance

Staying personal while automating enough to be efficient. This is precisely the gap an outsourced agent fills.

Where that leaves you

Operators that do well combine reliable systems, experienced staff, qualified chauffeurs, well-maintained vehicles, strong affiliate relationships and disciplined procedures. Four of those six are people doing things consistently — and on an overnight shift, a GroundOps agent is the one holding them up.

Lesson 11 of 11

1.11 Knowledge check

Knowledge check 01

Industry basics

Pass mark: 5 of 7.

A corporate executive assistant calls to book a car for her CEO; the company's accounts-payable department will be invoiced. Who is the passenger?

The assistant is the booking contact, AP is the billing contact, and the CEO — the person in the car — is the passenger.

A vehicle type has a 4-hour hourly minimum. A customer books it online for 2 hours. What happens?

Minimums are a gate on availability, not a rounding rule. The vehicle is filtered out, and depending on settings the customer sees "request a quote" or a hard stop.

You send a trip to a partner operator in Chicago because you have no cars there. That trip is a…

Work you send away is farmed out; the Chicago operator sees it as a farm-in.

"Fixed-or-distance" pricing means the system…

Fixed rates win when a zone pair exists; distance is the fallback for routes you haven't priced.

A client runs a black car operation. Which of these should you expect more of than on a chauffeured account?

Black car demand skews to immediate and near-term corporate work, and dispatch turns on availability and proximity. Advance planning, presentation and active monitoring characterise the chauffeured model.

At which stage of the reservation-to-billing workflow is an incorrect terminal cheapest to fix?

At confirmation it costs one question. At service delivery it costs a failed pickup, and by billing it is a dispute. Almost everything this academy asks of you is an attempt to move errors earlier in that list.

What is deadhead?

It is why "the driver is thirty minutes away" and "the car arrives in thirty minutes" are not the same statement, and why a same-day request needs the drive to the pickup counted in.
Phase 1 · Chauffeured transportation industry fundamentals

Transportation terminology

≡ Syllabus · Phase 1 · Module 2
≈ 10 min
≡Definition

Every industry has a shorthand. Ground transportation has about forty words that carry precise operational meaning, and customers, drivers and dispatchers all use them assuming you know them.

Getting one wrong is not a vocabulary slip — it changes what gets booked. "As-directed" and "point-to-point" are different products at different prices.

»Example

A caller says "I need the car on standby for four hours." "Standby" is not a service type. What she wants is as-directed / hourly, minimum four hours — a different rate table entirely from the airport transfer she booked last week.

✓Key points
  • Learn these before you take a live call
  • Several terms mean money: wait time, grace, no-show
  • Statuses are vocabulary too — they tell you where a trip is
  • When a caller uses a term loosely, restate it in the correct one
2.1 The words you will he…2.2 Status and workflow w…2.3 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 3

2.1 The words you will hear on every call

Vocabulary you will hear on every call

PU / DO
Pick-up and drop-off. "PU Date", "DO Time".
Spot time
When the driver should be in position, usually 15 min before PU.
Garage-out / Garage-in
Vehicle leaves and returns to base; used for hourly driver pay.
Farm-out / Farm-in
Sending a trip to, or receiving one from, an affiliate.
Meet & greet
Inside-terminal pickup with a name sign vs. curbside.
FBO
Fixed-base operator — a private-jet terminal. Its own routing type.
POI
Point of interest — a stored favourite place (stadium, hotel).
Direct bill
Corporate account invoiced on terms (e.g. net 30) instead of paying per trip.
Settle
Closing a done trip: confirm charges, driver/affiliate/agent pay, then file it.
ORES
Online Reservation System — the booking widget on the operator's website.
Advance reservation
A trip booked before the day or time of service — the opposite of ASAP.
ASAP
A trip wanted as soon as a suitable vehicle can get there. Module 13.
Base
The licensed or operating company that accepts and dispatches requests. The meaning varies by market, so check what a caller means by it.
Deadhead
Time or distance with no passenger aboard — driving to the pickup, or returning after drop-off. It is why "thirty minutes away" is not the same as "thirty minutes until pickup".
DMC
Destination management company — coordinates local transport, meetings, events and tours for a visiting group.
Garage time
Billable or operational time for travel from or back to the garage, depending on company policy and rate structure. Recorded as Gar-Out and Gar-In.
Knock-off
In some black car operations, the call telling the passenger their car is assigned or approaching, usually with the car number and an ETA.
Late cancellation
A cancellation inside the company’s chargeable window. A separate status from an ordinary cancellation, because it usually bills.
POB
Passenger on board — the driver status meaning the passenger is in the vehicle. Shown in Limo Anywhere as Customer In Car.
Point-to-point
One pickup to one destination, as opposed to hourly service.
Preferred traveler account
A retail-style account used to book travellers who have no direct-bill corporate account of their own.
Recurring / standing order
A reservation that repeats on a set schedule. Built once and repeated — so an error in it repeats too. Lesson 12.9.
STC
Surface transportation charge — an administrative fee covering permits, operating costs or similar, depending on company policy.
Transfer
A one-way trip between two points, commonly priced at a fixed or established transfer rate.
Voucher
A paper or electronic trip record used to authorise, document or bill a trip.
Lesson 2 of 3

2.2 Status and workflow words

In plain words — A trip's status is the single word that tells you where it is in its life. Half the questions you will be asked — "has he been picked up?", "is anyone on this yet?", "can I still cancel?" — are answered by reading one status field.

Office statuses

StatusWhat it meansWhat you can still do
QuoteA price has been given. Nothing is booked and no car is held.Everything. Convert it, revise it, let it expire.
UnassignedA real reservation exists, but no driver has been put on it.Change anything. Assign a driver.
Dispatched / OfferedThe trip has been sent to a driver who has not yet accepted it. Limo Anywhere carries both words as separate statuses; either way, nobody has committed yet.Change it, but tell dispatch — the driver is looking at the old version.
AssignedA driver has accepted. This trip has a name attached to it.Change it, then make sure the driver is told. Do not assume the app pushes it.
DoneThe ride happened. Charges may not be final.Correct charges, add tolls, fix wait time.
SettledClosed out: charges, driver pay and affiliate pay all recorded.Very little. Changing a settled trip is a deliberate accounting act — escalate.
CancelledCalled off. May still carry a cancellation charge.Nothing operationally. Check whether a charge applies.
No-showThe car was there; the passenger was not.Nothing without approval. No-show billing is a client policy decision.

Driver statuses

These arrive from the driver's phone, not from the office. When a passenger asks "where is my car?", this is the sequence you are reading.

1On the wayThe driver has started toward the pickup. This is the first moment you can give a passenger a real answer.
2CirclingOptional, and mostly an airport thing — the driver is in the cell lot or circling arrivals waiting for the passenger to land or clear.
3Arrived / On locationThe car is at the pickup point. If the passenger says otherwise, the two of them are in different places — that is a connection problem, not a lateness problem.
4Customer in carAlso called POB, "passenger on board". The pickup succeeded. Anything outstanding about the pickup can be closed.
5Passenger Dropped OffService complete. The trip becomes the office's problem again: charges, tolls, wait time, settlement.
A status is evidence, not a promise

"Arrived" means the driver pressed a button. It does not prove the car is at the right door. When a passenger and a status disagree, believe neither — get the driver's location and the passenger's location and compare them.

The farm-out family

A trip being driven by another company runs its own parallel set of statuses, so a dispatcher can tell at a glance which trips are theirs and which are somebody else’s. You will meet these constantly on affiliate work.

In-house statusFarmed-out equivalentWhat it means
UnassignedFarm-out UnassignedSent to an affiliate, not yet accepted by them.
AssignedFarm-out AssignedThe affiliate has accepted the trip.
—Affiliate Driver AssignedThey have put a named driver on it. This is the point at which you can tell a passenger who is collecting them.
On the wayFarm-Out On the WayTheir driver has set off.
CirclingFarm-out CirclingWaiting at the airport.
ArrivedFarm-out ArrivedTheir driver is at the pickup.
Customer In CarFarm-out Customer In CarThe passenger is aboard.
CancelledCancelled by AffiliateThey have handed it back. This is an exception — escalate it.
Why the duplication matters to you

On a farmed trip these statuses are usually set by hand, from whatever the affiliate tells you, because their system does not talk to your board unless the work came through LA Net. A farm-out trip sitting silently at Farm-out Unassigned the evening before is not a quiet trip — it is one nobody has accepted. Module 19 covers setting these by hand, and Module 22 covers chasing the affiliate.

The other statuses you will see

Driver Waiting at Stop

The driver is holding at an intermediate stop rather than the pickup. Wait time may be running.

Late Cancel

Cancelled inside the client’s charging window. Distinct from Cancelled, because it usually bills.

No Show

The car waited out the grace and nobody appeared. Never set this yourself without approval — Module 9 explains why.

Three words that decide money

Wait time

Billable time the driver spends waiting beyond the free allowance. Starts at the scheduled pickup, or at flight arrival plus the grace period on an airport job.

Grace period

The free waiting window before wait time starts — commonly 15 minutes for a local pickup and 30 to 60 minutes after a flight lands. Set per client.

No-show

The car waited out the grace and the passenger never appeared. It is usually billable in full, and it is almost always a decision someone senior confirms.

Lesson 3 of 3

2.3 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Terminology

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

A caller asks for "a car on standby all afternoon, we're not sure where we're going". Which service type is she actually describing?

Buying the car and driver for a block of time with no fixed destination is hourly, also called as-directed. It prices from an hourly table with a minimum, not from a fixed route.

A trip shows status Dispatched. What does that tell you?

Dispatched means offered. Until it reads Assigned, nobody has committed to driving it — which matters a great deal at 05:00 for an 06:00 pickup.

A flight lands at 14:10. The client's airport grace period is 45 minutes. From what time does billable wait time run?

On an airport arrival the clock starts at actual landing time, and the grace period runs from there. 14:10 plus 45 minutes is 14:55.

You send a trip in a city where your client has no vehicles to a partner operator who will drive it. From your client's point of view that trip is a…

Work you send away is farmed out. The receiving operator records the same trip as a farm-in.
Phase 1 · Chauffeured transportation industry fundamentals

Vehicle & service knowledge

≡ Syllabus · Phase 1 · Module 3
≈ 15 min
≡Definition

A vehicle type is a class of car the operator sells — Sedan, SUV, Sprinter — not a specific car. Rates, availability and online booking all hang off the type, and the actual registration plate is chosen later by dispatch.

Your job on a call is to match what the customer needs to the right class, first time.

»Example

"Four of us, coming from London, a week each." Four passengers fits a sedan — the luggage does not. Four international suitcases plus carry-ons is an SUV, and quite possibly a Sprinter.

✓Key points
  • Luggage decides the vehicle more often than passenger count does
  • Every stated capacity is a maximum, not a comfortable load
  • Child seats, wheelchairs and oversized items must be asked about, not assumed
  • When you are between two classes, price both and let the customer choose
3.1 The vehicle classes3.2 Passengers, luggage a…3.3 Choosing the right ve…3.4 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 4

3.1 The vehicle classes

Names vary between operators — "executive sedan", "first class sedan", "luxury sedan" may all be the same car. What does not vary is the shape of the ladder. Learn the ladder; check each client's own names in their module.

ClassTypical passengersTypical luggageWhat it is actually for
Sedan2–32 large + 2 smallThe default. One or two business travellers, a short airport run, a night out for a couple.
Premium / luxury sedan2–32 large + 2 smallSame capacity, better car (S-Class, 7 Series). Bought for the impression it makes, not the space.
SUV4–64–5 largeThe workhorse. Families, golf clubs, ski gear, four people with real suitcases, bad weather.
Passenger van7–12Varies — often shared with seatsGroups on a budget. Comfortable enough for an airport shuttle, not for a two-hour transfer.
Sprinter8–14Good, in a dedicated bayExecutive group travel. Stand-up headroom, rear luggage bay, often wifi and conference seating.
Stretch limousine6–10Very littleOccasions: weddings, proms, anniversaries. Almost never the right answer for an airport run.
Mini coach18–30Under-floor baysConference shuttles, wedding guest movements, corporate outings.
Motor coach40–56Large under-floor baysFull group movements, long distance, restroom on board on the larger units.
A stretch limousine is not a big SUV

It seats ten and carries almost no luggage — the boot is largely taken up by the stretch. A caller who says "limo" usually means "nice car", not a stretch. Ask what the occasion is before you book one.

Lesson 2 of 4

3.2 Passengers, luggage and the limits that bite

In plain words — The number on the spec sheet is the number of seat belts. It is not the number of people who will be comfortable, and it says nothing at all about where their bags go. Most vehicle upgrades happen at the kerb, in front of the customer, because nobody asked about luggage.

The luggage rule

Work it out in large bags — a checked suitcase. Two carry-ons count as one large. Then apply the class table. A sedan takes two large plus two small in the boot; a third large bag means someone's case rides on a seat, which on a premium booking is a complaint waiting to happen.

4 passengersfits a sedan on seats aloneOK
4 checked bagssedan holds 2 large + 2 smallFAILS
4 carry-ons as wellcounts as 2 more largeFAILS
Correct vehicleSUV, or two sedans if the client prefersSUV

The five questions that prevent an upgrade at the kerb

1 · How many passengers, including children?

Children occupy seats and often need seats fitted. "Two adults and a baby" is a three-seat booking with a car seat request.

2 · How many checked bags and how many carry-ons?

Ask for both. Customers report checked bags and forget the rest.

3 · Anything oversized?

Golf clubs, skis, cellos, pushchairs, boxes. Any one of these can move a sedan to an SUV on its own.

4 · Any child seats needed, and what age?

Limo Anywhere asks for one of three: rear facing (Infant), forward facing (Toddler) or Booster Seat, plus a count. Availability is limited — never promise one without checking the client's procedure.

5 · Any accessibility requirements?

Wheelchair access, a folding chair in the boot, a walker, room for a service animal. Wheelchair-accessible vehicles are a scarce, separately-booked resource.

Accessibility is never an assumption

If a caller mentions a wheelchair, do not guess whether a vehicle can take it. Establish whether the chair folds and whether the passenger can transfer to a seat, record the answers, and follow the client's procedure — which for a non-folding chair usually means a dedicated accessible vehicle booked well ahead, and often an affiliate.

Lesson 3 of 4

3.3 Choosing the right vehicle

Work down this ladder. Stop at the first rung that fails, and go up a class.

1SeatsDoes everyone have a belt, children included? If the count is at the vehicle's maximum, go up one class — a "6-passenger" SUV with six adults and bags is not a comfortable ride.
2LuggageConvert everything to large-bag equivalents. Compare against the class, not against the car you are picturing.
3Oversized and special itemsGolf clubs, skis, instruments, pushchairs, pets. Each one is a separate question, and any one can change the class.
4AccessibilityChair, walker, transfer assistance, service animal. If in doubt this is an escalation, not a judgement call.
5Occasion and account rulesA wedding wants the stretch; a board director's account may mandate premium sedan only. Client-specific vehicle requirements override everything above them.
6AvailabilityThe right class is no use if the operator does not have one free. If it is unavailable, offer the next class up with the price difference, or two smaller vehicles — whichever the client's procedure prefers.

Three calls, worked

"Two of us, JFK to midtown, hand luggage"

Sedan. Two passengers, two small bags. Nothing forces an upgrade. Quote the sedan and move on.

"Family of four, two weeks in Italy, two kids"

SUV, with two child seats. Four seats fit a sedan; four checked bags for two weeks do not, and the seats need fitting. Confirm seat ages.

"Nine of us to the conference, overnight bags"

Sprinter. A twelve-seat van technically fits nine, but nine overnight bags with the seats in place will not. The Sprinter's luggage bay is the reason it exists.

When you are between two classes, say so

"I can do that in an SUV at $180, or a Sprinter at $260 — the Sprinter gives you a separate luggage bay, which with nine bags I'd recommend." That is a better call than guessing, and it moves the decision to the person who knows what is in the bags.

Lesson 4 of 4

3.4 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Vehicles and service

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

Four adults are flying home after two weeks away: four checked bags and four carry-ons. What do you book?

Four checked bags plus four carry-ons is roughly six large-bag equivalents. A sedan takes two large plus two small. The seats fit; the luggage is what forces the SUV.

A caller says "we'd like a limo for my daughter's prom — eight girls". Which follow-up matters most?

A prom is an occasion booking: the vehicle is held for a block of time with multiple stops. It prices hourly with a minimum, and the itinerary is what you need.

A passenger uses a wheelchair. What is the correct first step?

A folding chair with a passenger who can transfer is often a normal booking with boot space; a non-folding chair needs a dedicated accessible vehicle. You establish the facts, then follow procedure — you neither guess nor refuse.

A vehicle type is listed as seating six. Six adults are travelling with one bag each. What is the sensible recommendation?

Stated capacity is a maximum. At the maximum with luggage it becomes an uncomfortable ride and often an upgrade at the kerb. Offer the choice, with the price, before the day.
Phase 2 · Customer service & communication

Answering customer calls

≡ Syllabus · Phase 2 · Module 4
≈ 30 min
≡Definition

Answering a call is a procedure, not a personality. Every call has the same six stages, and an agent who runs them in order sounds calm, finishes faster, and leaves a record someone else can pick up.

You are answering as the client's company. To the caller you are the limousine company.

»Example

"Good evening, Metro Executive Transportation, this is Priya, how may I help you?" — then, before anything else: who am I speaking to, and what do they need? Everything after that is just filling in fields.

✓Key points
  • Greet with the client's approved wording, every time
  • Identify the caller and the purpose in the first thirty seconds
  • Control the call: you ask the questions, in order
  • Never give out information about a booking to someone you have not identified
  • If it is not documented, it did not happen
4.1 The shape of a call4.2 Opening4.3 Control, listening an…4.4 Hold, transfer and wh…4.5 The nine kinds of call4.6 Closing and documenti…4.7 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 7

4.1 The shape of a call

Every call, from a two-minute cancellation to a twenty-minute group enquiry, runs through these six stages. Most bad calls are a stage skipped.

1GreetThe client's approved greeting, your name, an offer of help. Word-for-word as the client specifies — it is their brand, not yours.
2IdentifyWho is calling, what company, and are they an existing customer? Find their account before you find their problem.
3Establish the purposeOne of nine things. Say it back: "So you'd like to move tomorrow's 9am pickup to 10 — is that right?"
4Work itTake the booking, make the change, answer the question, take the message. This is the only stage that varies by call type.
5ConfirmRead back what will happen, in their words. Give the confirmation number. Say what they will receive and when.
6DocumentNote the interaction on the reservation or the account before you take the next call. Not at the end of the shift.
Stage 6 is the one that gets dropped, and it is the one that costs

An undocumented change is a change that the next agent, the dispatcher and the driver do not know about. When a passenger is standing at the wrong door at 05:00, the note you wrote at 22:00 is the only thing that explains why.

Roughly how long each stage takes

Greet and identifystages 1–220–30 s
Establish the purposestage 315–20 s
Work it — a changestage 41–2 min
Work it — a new reservationstage 43–5 min
Confirm and documentstages 5–645–60 s

If a call is running much longer than this, something has gone wrong in stage 3 — usually the purpose was never pinned down, and the call is wandering.

Lesson 2 of 7

4.2 Opening: greeting and identifying the caller

The greeting

Use the client's approved greeting exactly. It normally contains three parts, and each is there for a reason.

The company name

The caller needs to know they dialled correctly. Say the client's name, never "GroundOps" and never "hello".

Your name

Gives the caller someone to refer to and makes the call accountable. Use the name your client's procedure specifies.

An offer of help

"How may I help you?" hands the call over deliberately, rather than leaving a silence the caller has to fill.

Time of day matters

Many clients specify "Good morning / good afternoon / good evening" by their own local time, not yours. On an overnight shift from another time zone this is the single most common slip. Check the client's clock before your shift, not during your first call.

Identifying the caller

Before you can help anyone you need to know who they are and which account they belong to. Do this early — searching mid-sentence while a caller recites an address is how details get lost.

1Ask for the name"May I take your name?" Then the company if the greeting suggests corporate.
2SearchBy last name, company, phone number or confirmation number. A phone number is usually the fastest single search.
3Confirm you have the right record"I have you at the Fairmont on Tuesday — is that the one?" Never assume the first match is the right one.
4Read the account notes before you speak againAccount notes carry standing instructions: preferred vehicle, billing rules, "always call the assistant not the passenger". Reading them takes five seconds and prevents most errors.
Identify before you disclose

You may confirm details of a booking only to someone entitled to them. A caller who cannot give the passenger name, the confirmation number, or the account they book under does not get told where a car is or who is riding in it. Take a message and route it instead — this is a safety matter, not an administrative one.

Lesson 3 of 7

4.3 Control, listening and the questions that save time

In plain words — Call control is not talking over anyone. It is making sure that at every moment the call is on the question you need answered next. Callers volunteer information in the order it occurs to them; your job is to gather it in the order the reservation needs it.

Active listening, concretely

Acknowledge, briefly

"Right." "Understood." "I have that." Short signals that you are still there. Silence makes callers repeat themselves; long agreement makes calls twice as long.

Take the note as they speak

Type the address while they say it. Asking a caller to repeat an address they gave ninety seconds ago is the clearest possible signal that you were not listening.

Restate the decision, not the conversation

"So — SUV, 6am Thursday from the Hilton, to Dulles." Not a summary of the chat; a summary of what will be booked.

Listen for what was not said

A caller who books an airport pickup and gives no flight number has not finished. The gap is yours to notice, not theirs.

Steering a call that is drifting

SituationWhat to say
Caller is telling you the whole itinerary before you have their name"I'll get all of that — let me just take your name first so I can pull up your account."
Caller jumps between two different bookings"Let's finish Thursday's first and then I'll come straight to Friday."
Caller is upset about something you cannot fix"I understand, and I want to get this to the right person. Let me take the details so it goes over properly."
You need a moment to check something"May I put you on hold for about a minute while I check that?" — then wait for the answer.
Caller keeps adding to a request you have already confirmed"I've got the change in — is there anything else on this booking before I confirm it?"

Questions that save the most time

Ask these early and most calls shorten by a minute or two.

"Is this a new booking or a change to an existing one?"

Decides the whole shape of the call. Ask it in the first thirty seconds.

"Do you have a confirmation number?"

Turns a three-minute search into a three-second one.

"Is the passenger the same as last time?"

On corporate accounts, nine times in ten the answer is yes and you can skip four fields.

Lesson 4 of 7

4.4 Hold, transfer and what you may tell a caller

Hold

1Ask, do not announce"May I place you on hold for a moment while I check that?" Then wait for the answer. A caller who says no usually has a reason.
2Say how long"About a minute." Callers tolerate a known wait far better than an open one.
3Come back inside that timeIf you need longer, come back anyway: "I'm still checking — may I have another minute, or would you prefer I call you back?"
4Thank them on return"Thank you for holding." Then go straight to the answer. Do not restart the conversation.
Never hold a caller to avoid telling them something

If you do not know, say you do not know and say what you will do about it. A four-minute hold that ends in "I'll have to check and call you back" is worse than saying that immediately.

Transfer

Most GroundOps agents transfer rarely — usually to a client dispatcher, an accounting contact, or a senior agent. When you do, transfer warm wherever the client's procedure allows it.

Warm transfer

You speak to the receiving person first, explain who is holding and why, then connect them. The caller does not have to repeat themselves. This is the default.

Cold transfer

You put the call straight through. Only when the client's procedure specifies it, and never for an upset caller or an emergency — those are exactly the calls that must not be dropped into a voicemail.

Before you transfer, get a callback number

Transfers fail. If the line drops, the person you were helping is gone and you have no way to reach them. Take the number first, every time.

What you may tell a caller

This is the part most new agents get wrong, and it is the part with real consequences. The default is: confirm only to people entitled to know, and disclose only what they already have a right to.

CallerMay be toldMay not be told
The passenger, identifiedTheir own booking: time, vehicle class, driver first name, driver status, price on their own trip.Another passenger's booking, the driver's personal number unless the client permits it.
The booking contact / arranger, identifiedAnything on bookings made under their account, including the passenger's ride status.Bookings under other accounts at the same company unless their account covers them.
Someone claiming to be a relative or colleagueNothing about the booking. Take a message and route it.Whether the person is travelling, when, where from, or where to.
A driverTrip details for their own assignment.Account pricing, billing detail, other drivers' assignments.
An affiliateWhat the farmed trip requires: passenger name, timings, routing, contact for the day.Your client's retail price, account terms, or other customers.
"Is my husband's car booked for tonight?"

This is the question to be careful with. You do not confirm a person's movements to a caller who is not on the booking — however reasonable they sound, and however awkward it feels. "I'm not able to discuss a booking I can't confirm you're on, but I'll happily take a message for the account." That sentence is the whole answer.

Lesson 5 of 7

4.5 The nine kinds of call

Almost every call is one of these nine. Recognising which one you are on, early, tells you what the rest of the call looks like.

1 · New reservation

The longest routine call. Runs through the fifteen fields in Module 7. Ends with a confirmation number read back.

2 · Quote

A price request with no commitment yet. Gather the same information as a booking, price it, send it, document it, and note the follow-up.

3 · Reservation change

Find the booking first, then change it. Anything within a few hours of pickup needs the impact check in Module 13.

4 · Cancellation

Confirm which booking, cancel per procedure, and tell the caller plainly whether a charge applies. Never guess at the charge.

5 · Driver / status update

"Where is my car?" Read the ride status and the driver's position, then answer in times, not statuses. Module 17 covers the wording.

6 · Billing question

You can explain what a charge is. You do not adjust, waive or promise refunds. Route it to accounting with the trip number.

7 · Complaint

Listen, acknowledge, record the facts, do not defend. Route per the escalation matrix. Do not offer compensation.

8 · Message for someone

Take it completely — name, company, number, reason, urgency, what you already did — then route it. Module 6.

9 · Emergency / escalation

Breakdown, accident, stranded passenger, missed pickup, driver unreachable. Stop the routine and go to Module 20.

The call type can change mid-call

A status enquiry that reveals the driver is forty minutes out and the passenger is about to miss a flight has become an emergency. A cancellation where the caller is furious has become a complaint as well. When the type changes, change what you are doing — do not finish the original script first.

Deciding fast

1Is anyone stranded, unsafe, or about to miss something irrecoverable?Yes → type 9. Everything else waits.
2Is there an existing booking involved?No → types 1, 2 or 8. Yes → continue.
3Is the ride today or in progress?Yes → types 3, 5 or 9. No → types 3, 4 or 6.
4Is the caller unhappy about service already delivered?Yes → type 7, regardless of what else the call is about.
Lesson 6 of 7

4.6 Closing and documenting

Confirming

Read back the decision, not the conversation. The caller should be able to spot an error in ten seconds.

The read-back

"So that's Thursday the 14th, pickup 6:00am from 1400 Market Street, going to Dulles, in an SUV, for Mr Okafor, three passengers and four bags. Your confirmation number is 15449, and the confirmation email is going to you now. Is that all correct?"

Five things must appear in every read-back: the date, the time, the pickup address, the vehicle class and the passenger name. On an airport job, add the flight. Say the date as a weekday and a number — "Thursday the 14th" catches the mistake that "the 14th" alone does not.

Closing

Say what happens next

"You'll have the confirmation within a few minutes, and the driver's details the evening before."

Ask once whether there is anything else

Once, not twice. Twice sounds like you want the call to end.

Close in the client's name

"Thank you for calling Metro Executive." The call opened with the client's name; it should close with it.

Documenting

Write the note before you take the next call. A note written at the end of a shift is a note written from memory.

A note needsExample
Who called and when03 Sep 21:14 — call from Dana Whitfield (assistant, Vertex Group)
What they asked forAsked to move Thu 14th 06:00 PU to 07:00
What you didPU time amended to 07:00; revised confirmation sent to dana.w@vertex.com
What is still outstandingDriver already assigned — dispatch notified by note; Dana to confirm flight number tomorrow
Who you toldNote added for dispatch; nothing escalated
Where the note goes matters

A note about this trip goes on the reservation. A note about this customer generally — "always call the assistant, never the passenger" — goes on the account, where it will repeat on every future booking. Putting a standing instruction on one reservation means the next agent will never see it.

Lesson 7 of 7

4.7 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Answering calls

Pass mark: 4 of 5.

A caller says "Hi, I'm calling about my husband's car this evening — what time is it picking him up?" She is not on the booking and cannot give a confirmation number. What do you do?

Confirming a person's movements to someone not on the booking is a safety matter. Take a message and route it; the person on the booking can call back.

Which stage of a call is most often skipped, and what does skipping it cost?

Documentation is the stage with no immediate consequence and the largest delayed one. An undocumented change is invisible to everyone who needs it.

You need two minutes to check a rate. What is the correct handling?

Ask, estimate, return. Coming back to say "I need another minute" costs nothing and keeps the caller with you.

A caller rings to check a driver's whereabouts and mentions the passenger is elderly, waiting outside in the rain, and the car is 35 minutes late. What has this call become?

A vulnerable passenger exposed and a materially late car is a service failure in progress. The call type changed; what you do changes with it.

An account's standing instruction is "always contact the assistant, never the passenger directly". Where should that note live?

Standing instructions belong on the account. On a single reservation they disappear the moment that trip is done.
Phase 2 · Customer service & communication

Email communication

≡ Syllabus · Phase 2 · Module 5
≈ 20 min
≡Definition

Email is the other half of the job. Most corporate bookings, most quote requests and almost all group enquiries arrive as text, in a shared inbox that several agents work at once.

Email has one advantage over the phone — you can check before you answer — and one disadvantage: everything you write is permanent and forwardable.

»Example

"Can you do a car Thursday morning for Mr Reyes, IAD?" — four facts, six missing. A good reply books what it can, asks for the rest in a numbered list, and gives a time by which you need it.

✓Key points
  • Claim a message before you work it, so two agents don't reply twice
  • Answer the question that was asked, first, in the first line
  • Never leave a mail read-but-unanswered at the end of a shift
  • Every email that results in a booking gets noted on the reservation too
5.1 Working a shared inbox5.2 Reading an email for…5.3 Writing the reply5.4 Four worked examples5.5 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 5

5.1 Working a shared inbox

In plain words — A shared inbox is not your inbox. Several agents across several shifts are looking at the same list, so the discipline is about making your state visible: what you have taken, what you have answered, and what is waiting on somebody else.

The four states a message can be in

Unclaimed

Nobody has touched it. Anyone may take it.

Claimed

You have taken it — flagged, assigned or moved per the client's method. Nobody else should start work on it.

Waiting

You have replied and need something back: a flight number, an approval, a price from the client. It is not finished.

Done

Answered, actioned and documented. Filed per procedure.

Claim before you work

The most common shared-inbox failure is two agents replying to the same customer with two different answers. Claim it first, even for a message you expect to answer in ninety seconds.

Working the inbox

1Scan the whole list before answering anythingOldest first is not the right order. Something arriving twenty minutes ago about a pickup in an hour outranks a quote request from yesterday.
2Sort by when it bites, not when it arrivedToday's rides, then tomorrow's, then everything else. A change request for a trip in progress is not an email task — pick up the phone.
3Claim, work, reply, documentThe reservation gets a note as well as the customer getting a reply. The inbox is not the record.
4Leave the inbox in a state someone else can readAnything still waiting goes into the shift handoff by name and by what it is waiting for.

Response-time expectations

Every client sets their own; these are the shapes they usually take. Check the client's module for the real numbers.

TypeTypical targetIf you cannot meet it
Anything about a ride todayImmediately — and usually by phone, not emailEscalate. Do not let it sit.
Reservation or change request15–30 minutesSend a holding reply that says when you will have it.
Standard quoteWithin the hour, or same business dayAcknowledge and give a time.
Groups & events enquiryAcknowledge within the hour; full quote may take longerAcknowledge, then hand to a specialist per procedure.
Billing questionAcknowledge, then route to accountingNever answer it yourself with a number you are not sure of.
An acknowledgement is not an answer, and it is not nothing

"Thanks — I'm checking availability for Thursday and will confirm within the hour" stops a customer chasing, buys you time, and is the correct reply when the real answer is not available yet.

Lesson 2 of 5

5.2 Reading an email for purpose and urgency

Read every email twice before replying: once for what it asks, once for what it does not say. The gap is usually where the work is.

Purpose: which of the nine is it?

The same nine types as a call — new reservation, quote, change, cancellation, status, billing, complaint, message, emergency. Identify it before you start typing, because it decides both the reply and whether email is the right channel at all.

Some emails are not email tasks

An email about a ride happening in the next few hours, a cancellation for today, or anything with the word "urgent" from someone who does not use it lightly — pick up the phone, then reply in writing to leave the record. A customer who emails about a car that is late is not choosing email; they are using the last channel they had open.

Urgency: when does it bite?

SignalWhat it means
Ride is today or tomorrow morningHighest. Work it now, whatever else is in the list.
Driver, passenger or "waiting" appears in the textSomething is happening right now. Read it fully before touching anything else.
A third or fourth message in the same threadThe customer is chasing. The clock started when the first one arrived, not the latest.
Sent outside the sender's working hoursUsually means it was on their mind late — often a change to something imminent.
Marked urgent, from a sender who never doesBelieve them.
Marked urgent, from a sender who always doesJudge on content, not on the flag.

What is missing

Almost every emailed booking request is incomplete. Check it against the fifteen fields in Module 7 before you reply, and ask for everything missing in one message. Three separate emails asking for one thing each is how a Thursday booking becomes a Wednesday panic.

"Car Thursday morning for Mr Reyes, IAD"4 facts
Missingarrival or departure? flight? pickup address? time? passengers? bags? vehicle? payment?8 gaps
Right replyone message, numbered questions, a deadline1 email
Lesson 3 of 5

5.3 Writing the reply

The shape of a reply

1Answer firstThe first line answers the question asked. Not "thank you for your email" — "Yes, we can cover Thursday morning."
2Give the detailWhat is booked, or what it will cost, in a form that can be scanned: labelled lines, not a paragraph.
3Ask for what is missing, numberedNumbered questions get numbered answers. Prose questions get one answer and seven omissions.
4Say what happens next, and when"Once I have the flight number I'll send the confirmation." The customer should never have to ask what the state is.
5Sign off in the client's nameTheir signature block, their company, your first name.

Writing rules

Short sentences, labelled facts

Dates, times, addresses and prices go on their own lines with a label. A customer checking a booking on a phone should find the pickup time without reading a paragraph.

Dates in full

"Thursday 14 September" — never "14/9" (ambiguous internationally) and never "Thursday" alone.

Times with the zone when it could matter

Airport work crosses zones. "6:00am local" costs three words and prevents a missed flight.

No internal language

"Farm-out", "unassigned", "settled" are your words, not the customer's. Say "our partner operator in Chicago", "the driver hasn't been allocated yet", "the trip's been closed out".

Never promise what you cannot authorise

No refunds, no waived charges, no "we'll make it up to you". Say what you will do: "I'm sending this to the operations manager today."

Assume it will be forwarded

To the passenger, to a manager, into a complaint. Write every email as though the client's owner will read it, because sometimes they do.

Apologies

"I'm sorry that happened" acknowledges the customer's experience and is always safe. "I'm sorry we failed to dispatch a driver" is an admission on the client's behalf that may not be accurate and is not yours to make. Acknowledge the experience; report the facts; let the client characterise the cause.

Lesson 4 of 5

5.4 Four worked examples

Four messages you will see on nearly every shift, and a reply that works. Adapt the wording to the client's house style — the structure is what matters.

1 · An incomplete booking request

ReceivedReply
"Can you do a car Thursday morning for Mr Reyes, IAD?"

Yes, we can cover Thursday morning.

So I can confirm and price it, could you let me know:

1. Is this a pickup from Dulles, or a drop-off to Dulles?
2. If arriving — the airline and flight number.
3. If departing — the pickup address and the time he'd like to be collected.
4. Number of passengers and bags.
5. Any vehicle preference (we'd suggest a sedan for one or two).

If I have those by 4pm today I'll have the confirmation back to you the same afternoon.

Note what the reply does not do: it does not guess at arrival vs departure, and it does not book anything provisional that would then need unpicking.

2 · A change to an existing booking

ReceivedReply
"Tomorrow's 9am needs to move to 10am."

Done — tomorrow's pickup has moved to 10:00am.

Confirmation: 15449
Date: Thursday 14 September
Pickup: 10:00am, 1400 Market Street
Destination: Dulles International
Vehicle: SUV

A revised confirmation is on its way to you. The driver has been re-notified of the new time.

Find it before you promise it

If the account has two bookings tomorrow, "tomorrow's 9am" is not unambiguous. Reply with the confirmation number in the read-back so an error surfaces immediately rather than at 09:00.

3 · A quote request

ReceivedReply
"What would it cost to get four people from the Ritz to JFK on the 22nd, around 2pm?"

For four passengers from The Ritz-Carlton to JFK on Friday 22 September at 2:00pm:

SUV — $195.00 including gratuity, tolls and airport fees.
Sedan — $150.00, suitable for up to two large bags.

With four passengers I'd recommend the SUV unless they're travelling light.

This quote holds until 20 September. Shall I book it? If so I'll need the lead passenger's name and mobile number.

4 · A complaint

ReceivedReply
"Our driver was 25 minutes late this morning and my CEO missed a meeting. This is the second time."

Thank you for telling me, and I'm sorry that happened this morning.

I've recorded the details of today's trip (confirmation 15412, 7:00am pickup) and I'm sending this to the operations manager now, together with your note that this is the second occurrence.

Someone will come back to you directly. If it's useful in the meantime, I can put a note on the account to flag future pickups for this passenger for monitoring — just say the word.

What that reply avoids

It does not explain why the driver was late, does not blame traffic or the driver, does not offer a refund or a discount, and does not promise it will not recur. It acknowledges, records, routes and offers the one thing the agent can actually do.

Lesson 5 of 5

5.5 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Email communication

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

An email arrives at 05:50 saying "driver not here, flight was at 8, what's happening?" What is the correct first action?

A live service failure is not an email task. The customer used email because it was to hand. Call, fix, then write it down.

A booking request is missing five pieces of information. What is the best reply?

One message, numbered, with a deadline. Serial questions stretch a booking across days and lose information in the gaps.

A customer complains that a driver was late and their meeting was missed. Which sentence is appropriate in your reply?

Acknowledge the experience, record the facts, route it. Do not diagnose the cause, do not defend, and do not offer money you cannot authorise.

You have replied to a customer asking for a flight number before you can confirm. What state is that message in, and what must happen at end of shift?

Replied is not finished. Anything outstanding is "waiting" and must be handed over explicitly, or it falls into the gap between shifts.
Phase 2 · Customer service & communication

Messages, follow-up & escalation

≡ Syllabus · Phase 2 · Module 6
≈ 15 min
≡Definition

A message is what you take when the person who can answer is not you. An escalation is what you do when the person who should answer needs to be woken up.

The skill is telling the two apart quickly, and taking a message so complete that the next person needs no second call.

»Example

"Tell Mike the invoice is wrong" is not a message. "Dana Whitfield, Vertex Group, 214-555-0117, says invoice 8841 charges 3 hours' wait on trip 15402 and she believes the flight landed early. Wants a call back today. I have not adjusted anything." — that is a message.

✓Key points
  • Six fields make a message complete
  • Urgency is about consequence and timing, not tone of voice
  • Resolve what you are authorised to resolve; route the rest
  • Never sit on something because you are unsure whether it qualifies
6.1 What a complete messa…6.2 Judging urgency6.3 Resolve it, or escala…6.4 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 4

6.1 What a complete message contains

A complete message has six fields. Miss one and somebody has to make a second call — usually to a customer who has already explained themselves once.

1WhoFull name, company, and their role if it matters. "Dana Whitfield, executive assistant, Vertex Group."
2How to reach themDirect number and email, and when they are reachable. A mobile at 23:00 is not the same as a switchboard.
3What it is aboutThe subject in one line, with the trip, invoice or account number attached. Numbers save the recipient a search.
4What they want to happenA call back? An amendment? A decision? Ask if they have not said — "what would you like me to ask them to do?"
5By when"Today", "before the 6am pickup", "no rush, this week". This is what turns a message into a priority.
6What you have already doneThe field that gets left out, and the one that prevents duplicate work. "I have checked the trip and not changed anything."
Write it as if you will not be there to explain it

You will not be. The person reading your message is on a different shift, possibly a different continent, with no memory of the call. Everything they need has to be in the text.

The same message, badly and well

Badly

"Customer called about billing, wants a call back. Seemed annoyed."

Which customer? Which invoice? Which trip? Call back on what number, by when? And "seemed annoyed" is an impression, not a fact.

Well

"03 Sep 21:14 — Dana Whitfield, EA, Vertex Group. Direct 214-555-0117, dana.w@vertex.com, reachable 8–6 CT. Re: invoice 8841, trip 15402 (28 Aug, IAD arrival). Says 3 hrs wait time was charged but she believes the flight landed early. Wants a call back today from accounting. I have reviewed the trip, made no changes, and told her accounting would contact her."

Lesson 2 of 4

6.2 Judging urgency

In plain words — Urgency is not how loud someone is. It is the answer to one question: what happens, and how soon, if nobody acts? A calm caller whose 05:00 airport pickup has no driver is more urgent than a furious one disputing a charge from last month.
LevelTestAction
NowSomeone is stranded, unsafe, or a ride is failing in the next few hours and nobody has been told.Do not take a message. Go to Module 20 and escalate live, by phone, to the named contact.
TodayA ride in the next 24 hours is affected, or a customer is waiting on a decision that blocks their travel.Route it immediately to the right person by the method they actually read, and chase if it is not acknowledged.
This shiftNeeds an answer before the customer's next working day, but nothing fails tonight.Route it and put it in the handoff.
RoutineA question, a records correction, a future booking enquiry. Nothing is at risk.Route it through the normal channel. Still document it.

Signals that raise urgency

Time proximity

The nearer the pickup, the less slack there is. Anything inside four hours is at least "today".

Irrecoverability

A missed flight, a missed board meeting, a wedding. These cannot be re-run later at leisure.

Vulnerability

An elderly or unaccompanied passenger, a child, someone waiting outside at night or in bad weather.

Repetition

"This is the third time." Repeat failures are an account-level risk, not just an incident.

Silence from the driver

A driver who cannot be reached on an imminent job raises everything by one level immediately.

Money at scale

A disputed $40 toll is routine. A disputed $9,000 group invoice is not.

When in doubt, level up

The cost of over-escalating once is a mildly irritated supervisor. The cost of under-escalating once is a passenger left at an airport at midnight. These are not symmetrical, and you should not treat them as though they are.

Lesson 3 of 4

6.3 Resolve it, or escalate it

What you resolve yourself

The exact boundary is set by each client and lives in their module. This is the usual shape of it.

Normally yours to do

  • Take a new reservation within standard rates and availability
  • Make routine changes to a future booking
  • Answer "where is my driver" and give a status
  • Send a confirmation, a quote or a trip sheet
  • Cancel per the client's stated policy
  • Add notes, flag a follow-up, take a message

Normally not yours to do

  • Waive, discount or refund anything
  • Approve a no-show charge
  • Commit to a rate that is not in the system
  • Authorise an upgrade at the operator's cost
  • Change a settled trip
  • Promise a specific driver or vehicle
  • Accept a group booking that needs vehicles the operator does not have free

Who it goes to

Every client provides an escalation matrix. Module 21 covers how to read one; these are the roles it will name.

RoleWhat goes to them
GroundOps senior agentAnything you are unsure of; the first stop for most questions. Fastest route to an answer.
GroundOps supervisorRepeat problems, a customer asking for a manager, anything involving another agent's work.
Client dispatcherDriver and vehicle problems, live ride exceptions, same-day operational approvals.
Client operations managerService failures, unusual operational decisions, anything the dispatcher cannot authorise.
Client accountingInvoices, disputed charges, refunds, payment method problems.
Client general manager / ownerOnly per the matrix — typically a major service failure, or an emergency out of hours.
Designated emergency contactAccident, breakdown, stranded passenger, driver unreachable. Defined in advance, called without hesitation.
Escalating is not handing the problem away

You stay on it. Keep working what you can, keep the customer informed, and keep the record updated until somebody explicitly takes it from you. "I've escalated it" is not a closing state — "the operations manager has it and has spoken to the customer" is.

Three phrases worth having ready

To the customer

"That's not something I'm able to authorise, but I'm sending it to the person who can, now — and I'll stay on it until you've heard back."

To a senior person, out of hours

"I'm sorry to call at this hour. Passenger stranded at DFW, driver unreachable for 20 minutes, flight landed 40 minutes ago. Here's what I've tried."

To yourself, when unsure

"If this goes wrong, would somebody ask why I didn't call?" If yes, call.

Lesson 4 of 4

6.4 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Messages and escalation

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

Which of these is missing from an otherwise complete message: name, company, callback number, subject with trip number, what they want, by when?

"What I have already done" is the sixth field and the one most often dropped. Without it the next person repeats your work or, worse, undoes it.

Two calls come in together: a customer shouting about a charge on a two-month-old invoice, and a calm assistant whose 05:30 pickup tomorrow has no driver assigned. Which is more urgent?

Urgency is consequence and timing, not volume. The invoice can be resolved tomorrow; the unassigned early pickup cannot.

A regular corporate customer asks you to waive a $75 cancellation charge "as a goodwill gesture, we book with you every week". What do you do?

Waiving charges is not an agent decision. Neither is refusing on the client's behalf. Record it, route it, and tell the customer honestly what you have done.

You escalate a stranded-passenger situation to the client's emergency contact. What is your state afterwards?

Escalation adds a person; it does not remove you. You hand over when someone confirms they have it, not when you send the message.
Phase 3 · Reservation & product knowledge

Reservation fundamentals

≡ Syllabus · Phase 3 · Module 7
≈ 20 min
≡Definition

Before you touch any software, a reservation is a list of fifteen facts. Gather all fifteen and the booking is safe. Miss one and it fails somewhere between here and the kerb.

This module is about the facts. Module 12 is about where they go on the screen.

»Example

Everything correct — passenger, time, address, vehicle — but nobody asked for a mobile number. The driver arrives, cannot find the passenger, and has no way to call. One missing field, one failed ride.

✓Key points
  • Fifteen fields; some are required, all are useful
  • Ask in a fixed order so nothing is skipped
  • Read back before you finish, in the caller's own terms
  • A booking with gaps is a booking with a follow-up, and the follow-up is yours
7.1 The fifteen things ev…7.2 Verifying and reading…7.3 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 3

7.1 The fifteen things every reservation needs

Ask in this order. It follows the shape of the trip, which is how callers think about it, and it puts the two required fields near the front.

#FieldWhy it matters / what to watch
1Booker / contactWho is arranging it and how to reach them. On corporate work this is who gets the confirmation and every subsequent call.
2PassengerName as the driver will say it. Often not the caller. Get the spelling if it goes on an airport name board.
3Passenger mobileThe single most valuable field on the booking. Without it a driver who cannot find the passenger has no recourse.
4Pickup dateSay the weekday as well as the number. "Thursday the 14th" catches errors that "the 14th" does not.
5Pickup timeRequired. On airport arrivals the flight drives this — see Module 8. Confirm am/pm explicitly.
6Pickup locationFull address including suite, gate, door or terminal. "The Hilton" is not an address in a city with six of them.
7DestinationSame standard. On an hourly booking there may be none — that is a valid answer, not a gap.
8Additional stopsEach stop has an address, and often a wait. Stops change the price; ask rather than discover them on the day.
9Service typePoint-to-point, from airport, to airport, hourly, charter. This chooses the rate table, so getting it wrong misprices everything.
10Vehicle typeFrom Module 3. Driven by luggage at least as often as by passenger count.
11Passenger countIncluding children. Affects vehicle and sometimes price.
12LuggageChecked and carry-on, plus anything oversized. The field that prevents kerbside upgrades.
13Flight informationAirline and flight number on any airport job, arriving or departing. Not optional; it is what lets the trip track a delay.
14Special instructionsMeet & greet, child seats, accessibility, "call on arrival, don't ring the bell", water, a name board spelling.
