16.1 The dispatch board

Click the Dispatch icon and you get one table: every trip for the selected date, one row each. Change the date at the top to see another day. The row shows the essentials — confirmation number, pickup time, status, passenger, pickup and drop-off, vehicle type, driver and car — and its colour tells you the status at a glance (your company picks the colours).

Right-click = everything

Double-click = edit

16.2 Set up your grid

Every dispatcher can shape the board to their own eyes. Click Grid Setup on the Dispatch page. Five tabs; press Update Dispatch Grid Fields to save any of them.

Grid Setup — columns

Tick the columns you want, drag them up (left) or down (right), set widths in pixels. Tip: turn on Special System Notification Flags to get the ❗ column.

Date / Time

Date and time formats, the business hours the grid shows, and Refresh Dispatch Every — choose Auto Updates so changed trips glow on screen without you pressing refresh (must be enabled in company settings first).

Conflicts

On or off: warn when a driver or car is double-booked.

My Prefs — just for you

Hide statuses you don't need (e.g. Done), colour airport runs or VIPs, show contact info on hover, choose your map provider, font size, row height, and whether the whole row or only the status cell is coloured.

Company Prefs — for everyone

Which flags appear: unpaid balance, child seat, last-minute booking (you choose the window), driver rejected, Driver Anywhere messaging.

Filters & presets (new grid)

Column + Operator + Value, e.g. Driver · Equals · Darrell, or Conf# · Contains · 154. Save as a preset or a permanent tab such as "Airport runs today".

Lesson 3 of 3

16.3 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Dispatch fundamentals

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

What is the dispatch board actually showing you?

Reservations is the order book; Dispatch is the kitchen. It is a single day, everything on it, coloured by status.

A trip on today's board shows as Unassigned at 09:40 for an 11:00 pickup. What does that mean?

Unassigned means no driver. On a same-day trip it is the most urgent thing on the board, and it does not resolve itself.

Why does each dispatcher set up their own grid?

The grid is a working instrument. Showing the columns that matter for your role is how exceptions become visible instead of buried.

Where do most per-trip actions live on the dispatch board?

Right-clicking a row is the main working gesture on the board — assign, dispatch, change status, open, copy.
Phase 7 · Light dispatch

Tracking the driver

≡ Syllabus · Phase 7 · Module 17
≈ 20 min
≡Definition

Tracking the driver is the difference between answering "I don't know" and answering "he's eight minutes away, on Market Street". It is the most frequent live task on an overnight shift.

You are reading three things at once: the ride status, the driver's position, and the clock.

»Example

Status says On the way. The map puts the car 14 miles out. Pickup is in 12 minutes. That trip is going to be late, and nobody has told anyone yet. Spotting that before the passenger calls is the job.

✓Key points
  • A status is evidence, not proof
  • Compare position against time, not against the status
  • Tell the passenger before they ask, if you possibly can
  • Give times and places, never internal status words

17.1 Map, GPS and calendar

Map view & directions

The new grid's Map view plots today's pickups. On any grid, right-click a trip › Map to get directions from your chosen provider (Google Maps, MapQuest…) — set per user under My Prefs.

GPS tab

Every driver who is on duty in Driver Anywhere appears as a dot with speed and heading — no GPS hardware needed. Use it to answer "where is my car?" calls.

Calendar

Month, week, work-week or day views of the same trips, colour-coded by status, filterable by status, driver, car or vehicle type. Non-trip events (meetings, vehicle service) are added by hand. Defaults live under Company Preferences › Accounts, Calendar, Quotes.

Driver's side of the same picture

In Driver Anywhere the driver taps On duty, picks their car, sees Upcoming / In progress / Pending, and moves through the statuses in order (they can skip Circling but never go backwards). They can add notes, photos, wait time, tolls and — if allowed — take payment at the end. Everything they tap lands on your board.

Lesson 2 of 4

17.2 Is this driver going to be late?

In plain words — Lateness is arithmetic: where is the car, how long will it take, and how long is left. Do that sum early enough and a late ride becomes a managed one.

The three readings

1Ride statusHas the driver started? Unassigned or Dispatched close to pickup is a bigger problem than a driver who is merely behind.
2Driver positionWhere is the car now, and which way is it pointing? A car three miles out and stationary for ten minutes is not three minutes away.
3Time remainingAgainst the spot time, not the pickup time. The driver should be in position before the passenger comes out.

When to act

What you seeDo this
Still Unassigned inside 2 hours of pickupRaise it with dispatch now. This does not fix itself.
Dispatched but not accepted inside 60 minutesRaise it. Nobody has committed to this trip.
On the way, but position says it will not make the spot timeTell dispatch, and prepare to tell the customer. Do the sum before you are asked.
No status change for 20 minutes on a live tripContact the driver per procedure. Silence is information.
Arrived, but the passenger says there is no carNot a lateness problem — a connection problem. Establish both locations.
Driver unreachable on an imminent jobEscalate. Module 20.
Ten minutes late on an airport departure is not the same as ten minutes late on a dinner reservation

Weigh the consequence, not just the delay. A passenger with a 90-minute check-in cushion can absorb it. A passenger who is already tight cannot, and that call goes out immediately.

Getting the driver

Whether, when and how you contact a driver directly is set by each client. Some route everything through their own dispatcher; some let agents call. Know which before your shift.

Ask a closed question

"What's your ETA to the Hilton?" Not "are you running late?" — which invites a yes and no number.

Keep it to ten seconds

They are driving. Get the ETA, tell them anything they need, end the call.

Write down what they said

Their ETA, the time you called, what you told them. This becomes the record if the trip goes wrong.

Lesson 3 of 4

17.3 Telling the passenger

In plain words — Passengers do not want a status. They want to know when the car will be there and what to do in the meantime. Translate before you speak.

Translate the status

What the screen saysWhat you say
Assigned"Your driver's confirmed — that's Darrell in a black Suburban."
On the way"He's on his way to you now, about twelve minutes out."
Circling"He's waiting at the airport for you — he'll come round as soon as you're at the door."
Arrived"He's outside now, at the main lobby entrance on Market Street."
UnassignedNever say it. Say what you are doing: "I'm confirming your driver now and I'll come straight back to you."

Telling someone the car is late

1Call before they call youA passenger told at 06:48 that their 07:00 car will be ten minutes late is an inconvenienced customer. One who rings at 07:09 is a complaint.
2Give a real number"About twelve minutes." Not "shortly", not "any moment". If you do not know, say when you will know: "I'm confirming with the driver now — I'll call you back within five minutes."
3Say what you are doing about it"I've spoken to the driver and dispatch know." People tolerate delay far better than they tolerate the sense that nobody is on it.
4Ask about the consequence"Does that still work for your flight?" This is the question that decides whether this is a delay or an emergency.
5Call again when you said you wouldEven if the news has not changed. A promised call that does not come costs more than the delay did.
6Document itTimes, who you spoke to, what you were told, what you promised.
Do not explain why

"There was traffic", "the previous job overran", "the driver overslept" — none of these help the passenger and all of them commit the client to a version of events you cannot verify. Say what is happening and when the car will arrive. The cause is for the client to establish afterwards.

What you may give out

Normally fine

Driver's first name, vehicle make, colour and class, an ETA, where the car is waiting. These help the passenger find their car.

Check the client's rule

The driver's mobile number, the exact registration plate, the driver's live map position. Many clients share these; some do not, and it is not your judgement to make.

Lesson 4 of 4

17.4 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Tracking the driver

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

The status reads Arrived but the passenger says there is no car. What is the situation?

"Arrived" means a button was pressed. Most of these are two people in the same building on different levels. Get both locations and connect them.

A 07:00 pickup, and at 06:45 the car is clearly not going to make it. When do you call the passenger?

Calling before they call you converts a complaint into a managed inconvenience, and the question about consequence tells you whether this is now an emergency.

A passenger asks why their driver is late. What do you say?

Give the time, say what you are doing, and check the consequence. Explaining causes commits the client to a version of events you cannot verify.

A live trip has shown no status change for twenty minutes. What does that mean?

On a live job, no news is not good news. Twenty silent minutes is worth one ten-second call.
Phase 7 · Light dispatch

Driver wake-up calls

≡ Syllabus · Phase 7 · Module 18
≈ 12 min
≡Definition

A wake-up call is a scheduled call to a driver before an early assignment, to confirm they are awake, aware of the job, and going to make it.

It exists because the single most common cause of a failed early-morning pickup is a driver who slept through the alarm — and because nobody else is awake to notice.

»Example

04:15. Darrell has an 05:30 spot at the Fairmont. You call. No answer. You call again at 04:20. No answer. At 04:25 you escalate — because there is still time to put another driver on it, and in twenty minutes there will not be.

✓Key points
  • Call at the time the client specifies, not when you get to it
  • Confirm three things: awake, aware, and the time
  • Document every attempt, with times
  • Escalate early — the value of the call is the warning it gives
18.1 Why the call exists18.2 Making the call18.3 When a driver cannot…18.4 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 4

18.1 Why the call exists

In plain words — The wake-up call is not a courtesy. It is an early-warning system. Its value is not in waking the driver; it is in discovering, ninety minutes before a pickup, that a driver is not going to make it — while something can still be done.

Why so early

The call is scheduled to leave time to react. A call fifteen minutes before departure confirms a failure; one ninety minutes before prevents it.

Why a call, not a text

A text does not wake anyone and does not prove anyone read it. A voice on the phone proves a human being is conscious.

Why it is documented

When a pickup fails, the first question is whether the wake-up call was made. Your log is the answer.

Preparing the list

1Pull the schedule at the start of your shiftNot at 03:50. Know at 22:00 who you are calling and when.
2Identify who needs a callUsually driven by the client's rule — all assignments before a certain hour, or specific drivers who have asked for it, or those flagged on the schedule.
3Work out each call time from the spot timeThe client specifies the lead — commonly 60 to 90 minutes before the driver needs to leave. Write the call times down as a list.
4Check the assignments are still currentA driver reassigned at 23:00 should not get a call about a job they no longer have, and the new driver should.
5Set your own alarmsNothing in the system will remind you. A missed wake-up call is an agent error, not a system gap.
A wake-up call you forgot is worse than one that was never scheduled

The operator has built their morning on the assumption that a human will check. If the call does not happen, nobody finds out until a passenger is standing outside at 05:30.

Lesson 2 of 4

18.2 Making the call

The call, in about twenty seconds

1Identify yourself and the company"Morning Darrell, it's Priya from Metro Executive dispatch." At 04:15 a driver needs a second to work out who is calling.
2Say why"Your wake-up call for the 05:30 at the Fairmont."
3Confirm they are awake and upNot just answering. "Are you up?" A driver who answers half-asleep and goes back to sleep is a failure you have already logged as a success.
4Confirm they have the assignment"You've got the Fairmont pickup, 05:30 spot, going to DFW?" Read the key facts back; this catches reassignments they never saw.
5Confirm the timing works"Are you good for that?" A driver who says "I'm 40 minutes away and just getting up" has told you something important.
6Log itTime called, answered, what they confirmed. Immediately, not later.

Three things to listen for

Hesitation about the job

"Which one?" means they do not have it. Read it out and confirm they are writing it down.

Hesitation about the time

"I should be alright" is not "yes". Ask what time they will leave, and do the arithmetic yourself.

Anything about the vehicle

"I'll need to swing by the yard" or "the car's got a warning light" is a dispatch problem starting now, not at 05:30.

Answering is not confirming

The purpose is not to hear a voice; it is to establish three facts — awake, has the job, can make the time. If you did not establish all three, the call is not complete and should not be logged as though it were.

Lesson 3 of 4

18.3 When a driver cannot be reached

In plain words — The whole value of the wake-up call is the time it buys. A driver who does not answer is exactly the situation the call exists to detect, so the response is fast, defined and documented — not a series of hopeful redials.

The reattempt sequence

Each client sets their own intervals. This is the usual shape; use theirs.

1First call at the scheduled timeNo answer — log it with the exact time. Leave a voicemail stating the job and asking them to call back immediately.
2Second call after about five minutesAnd a text as well, so there is something to see when they wake.
3Third call after another fiveTry any alternative number on the driver record.
4Escalate — do not keep diallingTypically ten to fifteen minutes after the first attempt. Contact the client's dispatcher or designated on-call person.
5Keep trying while the escalation runsThe two happen in parallel. If the driver answers, tell whoever you escalated to straight away.
6Document all of itEvery attempt with its time, the voicemail, the text, who you escalated to and when they responded.
Escalate on the clock, not on a feeling

The temptation is to try once more, and then once more, because the driver "always answers eventually". Fifteen minutes of redialling is fifteen minutes the dispatcher did not have to find a replacement. Set the escalation time when you make the first call, and keep to it.

What you say when you escalate

The whole message in one breath

"Darrell Owens isn't answering for the 05:30 Fairmont pickup — that's a DFW departure for Mr Okafor. I've called at 04:15, 04:20 and 04:25, left a voicemail and a text, and tried his second number. No response. Spot time is in 65 minutes."

Who, which job, what the consequence is, what you have tried, and how much time is left. That is everything the person you have woken needs to make a decision.

Afterwards

Follow the outcome

If a replacement driver is assigned, make sure the reservation reflects it and the passenger is told if the timing has changed.

Note it on the driver record

Per the client's procedure. A pattern of unanswered wake-up calls is something the operator needs to see.

Put it in the handoff

Even if resolved. The incoming shift should know it happened, especially if the same driver has jobs later.

Lesson 4 of 4

18.4 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Driver wake-up calls

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

What is the actual purpose of a wake-up call?

Waking them is the easy part. The value is the warning — time for dispatch to find a replacement while that is still possible.

A driver answers, sounds half asleep, and says "yeah, fine". What have you established?

Answering is not confirming. Read the job back, ask what time they are leaving, and satisfy yourself on all three points before you log it.

Three calls, a voicemail and a text over ten minutes, and no response. What now?

Escalate on the clock. Every minute spent redialling is a minute dispatch does not have to arrange cover.

During the call a driver mentions the car has a warning light on. What is that?

You have just been handed 90 minutes' warning of a possible vehicle failure. Use it.
Phase 7 · Light dispatch

Light dispatch operations

≡ Syllabus · Phase 7 · Module 19
≈ 25 min
≡Definition

Light dispatch is monitoring and communication, not decision-making. You watch the day, you keep information moving between drivers, passengers and the client, and you raise what needs raising.

What you do not do is restructure the operation. The boundary is the most important thing in this module.

»Example

A driver is 20 minutes behind on a chain of three trips. Light dispatch spots it, tells the dispatcher and warns the affected passengers. Full dispatch decides to move trip three to another car. The second decision is not yours.

✓Key points
  • Monitor, communicate, document, escalate
  • Routine information to drivers: yes. Reassignment: no
  • Every communication gets logged
  • When you are unsure which side of the line you are on, you are on the far side

19.1 Dispatching: offering vs assigning a driver

≡Definition

A status is where a trip is in its life (Unassigned → Offered → Assigned → On the way … Done). Your company names them; each is mapped to one of Limo Anywhere's built-in states, and that mapping drives what happens.

»Example

Pick Darrell in the dropdown: nothing happens. Change status to Dispatched (mapped to "Offered to driver"): his phone buzzes with Accept / Reject. He accepts → status flips to Assigned by itself.

✓Key points
  • A driver name on the trip is a plan, not a dispatch
  • Offered = driver may accept or reject (contractors)
  • Assigned = no choice, straight to Upcoming (employees)
  • Mapping lives in System Settings › System Mapping; each status has a code, name and colour

Don't touch these

"Online and eFarm-in", "Dispatched" and "Cancelled by Affiliate" have special functions. Deactivate other statuses by dragging to Inactive or clicking ×.

Status-to-time mapping

Stamp times automatically: e.g. On the Way → Garage-out, Arrived → Spot time, Dropped off → DO time. Choose whether to overwrite times already saved.

Drivers can't go backwards

Driver Anywhere only offers the driver-flow statuses, in order; Circling is the one optional step. The office can set any status from the reservation or the dispatch grid.

Lesson 2 of 6

19.2 Assigning and dispatching a driver

Two separate things happen, and new agents mix them up. Putting a name on the trip — choosing a driver and a car in the row — is just the office's plan. Dispatching — changing the status — is what actually sends the job to the driver's phone. Nothing reaches the driver until the status changes.

1Pick driver + carChoose from the dropdowns in the row. The car must belong to the requested vehicle type, or you get a warning (not a block).
2AStatus → OfferedYour "Dispatched" status. Driver gets a push notification with Accept / Reject. Accept → status flips to Assigned by itself. Reject → back to Unassigned, driver cleared.
2BStatus → AssignedNo choice for the driver — the trip simply appears in their Upcoming list. Usual for employees; Offered is usual for contractors.
3Driver runs the flowOn the way → (Circling) → Arrived → Customer in car → Dropped off → Done. Each tap updates your board within seconds.
4Watch the exceptionsA trip stuck in Offered too long, a rejection, a flight delay, a conflict warning — those are the dispatcher's real job.

Statuses are your words, mapped to LA's

Your company may call it "Dispatched", "Code 10" or "Sent". What matters is which canonical state it is mapped to in System Settings › System Mapping. That mapping is what triggers the driver notification.

Conflicts

If Grid Setup › Conflicts is on, the board warns when the same driver or car is on two overlapping trips. It warns; it does not stop you.

Farm-outs on the board

A farmed-out trip shows the affiliate's statuses (Offered to affiliate → Affiliate assigned → Affiliate driver on the way…) when real-time updates are on for both companies.

Lesson 4 of 6

19.4 The boundary of light dispatch

In plain words — "Light" is doing a lot of work in the phrase "light dispatch". You keep the day visible and everybody informed. You do not make the operational calls that reshape it, because you cannot see the whole picture and you do not carry the liability.

Normally within light dispatch

  • Review upcoming rides and flag gaps
  • Monitor active rides and statuses
  • Confirm driver and vehicle assignments are in place
  • Check flight information and act on delays
  • Pass routine information to a driver — an address correction, a passenger's phone number, a gate change
  • Give passengers status and ETAs
  • Help a passenger and driver find each other
  • Identify late or potentially late rides
  • Make wake-up calls
  • Document every communication
  • Escalate exceptions

Normally beyond it

  • Assigning or reassigning a driver on your own judgement
  • Moving a trip to a different vehicle
  • Releasing a driver from a job
  • Deciding to farm a trip out
  • Authorising a driver to leave a pickup before the grace period ends
  • Deciding that a trip is a no-show
  • Telling a driver to break a rule — speed, hours, parking
  • Agreeing a change that affects another customer's trip
  • Committing the operator to a recovery cost
The rule when you are unsure

If your action would change which vehicle or which driver does a job, or would affect another customer's trip, it is not light dispatch. Raise it with the client's dispatcher and let them decide. Doing this costs one phone call; getting it wrong can strand two passengers instead of one.

The four verbs

1MonitorWork the board continuously. The exceptions you find yourself are the ones that get fixed cheaply.
2CommunicateDriver, passenger, client, in whatever order the situation needs. Nobody involved should learn about a problem from someone else.
3DocumentOn the trip, as it happens. Times, names, what was said, what was promised.
4EscalateAnything past the boundary, and anything you would be asked about later if it went wrong.

Working a shift

WhenWhat you sweep for
Start of shiftRead the handoff. Then scan the whole board: unassigned trips, early pickups, wake-up calls due, anything flagged.
Every 15–20 minutesActive rides and their statuses. Anything silent for 20 minutes. Flights due in.
Two hours before each early pickupIs it assigned? Is it accepted? Is the driver's wake-up call scheduled?
As each flight landsDid the driver's status move? Is the passenger connecting with them?
End of shiftEverything still open, by name, with what it is waiting for. Module 26.
Lesson 5 of 6

19.5 Manual dispatch: no app, or farmed out

In plain words — Everything on the dispatch board assumes the driver is holding a phone running Driver Anywhere. Plenty of trips are not like that: a driver who does not use the app, a driver whose phone has died, or a trip being driven by another company entirely. Those statuses do not update themselves — somebody has to set them by hand, and on an overnight shift that somebody is you.

When the driver is using the app

This is the normal case, and it is worth knowing exactly what the driver sees, because half of what you will be asked is "has he got it yet?"

1The offer arrivesDispatch sets the trip to Dispatched. The driver gets a push notification and the trip appears in Driver Anywhere with Accept and Decline. Nothing is committed yet.
2The driver acceptsThe board row changes from Dispatched to Assigned and the colour changes with it. That is the moment a human being has taken responsibility for the trip — not when it was offered.
3The driver runs the statusesFrom the trip screen in the app, in order: On the way → Circling (optional, mostly airports) → Arrived → Customer in car → Dropped off. Each tap writes back to the board within seconds.
4The driver closes the tripAfter drop-off the app asks for the closeout details — actual times, wait time, tolls, parking, extra stops, gratuity if taken in the car, and any pictures. Submitting that sets the trip to Done.
5The office settles itDone is not closed. What the driver reported is what you check in Module 23, and what you settle in Module 24.
Accepted does not mean moving

A trip can sit at Assigned for hours. It only tells you a driver said yes. The status that means a car is actually in motion is On the way — and on an early pickup, that is the one you watch for.

When the driver is not using the app

Some drivers are not set up on Driver Anywhere, some refuse to use it, and some have a dead phone at 04:00. The trip still needs a truthful status, because everything downstream — the passenger's answer, the settlement, the invoice — reads from it.

What happensWhat you do
Driver confirms the job by phone or textSet the status to Assigned by hand, and note how it was confirmed and when: "Confirmed by phone 04:18."
Driver says they are leavingSet On the way. Note the time they told you.
Driver reports arrivalSet Arrived, with the time.
Driver reports the passenger is aboardSet Customer in car.
Driver reports drop-offSet Dropped off, then take the closeout details verbally — actual times, wait, tolls, parking, stops — and record them on the trip.
Driver goes quiet mid-tripDo not advance the status on assumption. An invented status is worse than a stale one, because everyone downstream believes it.
Always mark a hand-entered status as hand-entered

A status you set from a phone call and a status the driver tapped in the app look identical on the board. Note the source and the time in the dispatch notes every time you set one by hand. When a trip is queried a week later, "Arrived 05:28 — set by agent, per driver's call" is evidence; an unexplained status is not.

When the trip is farmed out

On a farm-out there is no driver of yours and no app at all. The affiliate has the car, and their system does not talk to your board unless the work came through LA Net.

Through LA Net

Statuses can sync between the two operators automatically. Treat them as you would a driver's own updates — but confirm anything critical by phone rather than trusting a quiet board.

By email or phone

Nothing syncs. The trip sits at Farm-out unassigned until you change it, and every status on it is one you set by hand from what the affiliate tells you. Ask at the points that matter: driver allocated, on the way, passenger on board.

A farm-out with no updates is not a quiet trip — it is an unmonitored one

The absence of status changes on a farmed trip tells you nothing at all, because nothing was ever going to change it. Set your own reminders at the points you would have expected an update, and chase. Module 22 covers the coordination in full.

Lesson 6 of 6

19.6 Knowledge check

Knowledge check 05

Dispatch

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

You chose Darrell and car SUV-3 on a row and saved. Darrell says he never got the trip. Why?

Names on the row are the plan; the status change is the dispatch.

A trip has been in "Dispatched" (Offered) for 40 minutes. What does that tell you?

Offered means waiting for the driver's Accept. That visibility is the point of the status.

Where do you make the board colour VIP passengers, only for your own login?

My Prefs is per user; Company Prefs is for everyone.

A customer calls: "Where is my car?" Fastest way to see the driver's live position?

Phase 8 · Emergency response & escalation

Emergency & critical situation response

≡ Syllabus · Phase 8 · Module 20
≈ 25 min
≡Definition

An emergency is any situation where passenger safety, or the delivery of the service, is at immediate risk. It is not defined by how upset anyone is.

Your role is narrow and important: gather the facts, follow the client's procedure, contact the right person, keep communicating, and document everything. You do not improvise solutions on the operator's behalf.

»Example

02:40. A driver calls: the vehicle has broken down on the interstate with a passenger on board, 25 miles from the airport. You do not solve this alone, and you do not wait until morning. You gather, you escalate, and you stay on the line.

✓Key points
  • Safety first, always — emergency services before anything commercial
  • Gather facts before you act, but do not let gathering delay the escalation
  • Follow the client's procedure; do not invent one
  • Stay with it until somebody explicitly takes it from you
20.1 What counts as an eme…20.2 The response sequence20.3 Eight situations, wor…20.4 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 4

20.1 What counts as an emergency

In plain words — Ask two questions. Is anyone unsafe? and is this ride about to fail in a way that cannot be recovered? A yes to either makes it an emergency, whatever tone the call arrives in.
SituationWhy it is an emergency
AccidentInjury is possible. Emergency services and the client's named contact, immediately, in that order.
Vehicle breakdown with a passenger aboardPeople are stationary somewhere they did not choose, possibly unsafe. Recovery needs an operational decision now.
Driver unable to complete the assignmentIllness, a vehicle problem, an accident on a previous job. There is a passenger expecting a car that is not coming.
Passenger strandedNo car, at an airport or a kerb, possibly late at night, possibly abroad. The most common genuine emergency on an overnight shift.
Potential missed pickupNot yet failed — which is exactly why it is worth escalating now, while it can still be prevented.
Driver cannot be reachedOn a live or imminent job, silence means you cannot rule out an accident or a no-show. Both need somebody senior.
Significant flight disruptionA diversion or a cancellation that leaves a booked trip meaningless and a passenger in the wrong city.
Major service failureA high-value group movement collapsing, a VIP left waiting, multiple failures on one account in one day.
Safety outranks everything in this training

If there is an accident, an injury, a medical situation, or anyone in immediate danger, the correct first action is the local emergency number — not the client, not your supervisor, not a note on the reservation. Nothing in any client's procedure overrides that, and no client will ever fault you for it.

What is not an emergency

An angry caller

Volume is not urgency. A furious complaint about last month's invoice is a complaint, handled properly, today.

A ten-minute delay with slack in it

Manage it, communicate it, document it. It becomes an emergency only when the consequence becomes irrecoverable.

A billing dispute, whatever the amount

Route it to accounting. Money is recoverable; that is what makes it not an emergency.

Lesson 2 of 4

20.2 The response sequence

The same eight steps, whatever the emergency. Learn the sequence and you will never be improvising at 03:00.

1Establish whether anyone is hurt or in dangerFirst question, always. If yes — emergency services, now, before anything else. Confirm the location before you do anything else with the call.
2Stay calm and stay on the lineYour tone sets the tone. Short questions, one at a time. Do not put an emergency caller on hold.
3Gather the essential factsWho, where exactly, what happened, when, who is with them, what is the immediate risk. Location in the most precise form available — a mile marker, a terminal and door, a junction.
4Write it down as you goYou will be repeating this to two or three people in the next ten minutes. Write once, read many times.
5Contact the client's designated personFrom the escalation matrix. Out of hours, that is what the emergency contact is for — call it, without hesitation and without apologising at length.
6Keep the affected people informedThe passenger, the arranger, the driver. Short, factual updates. "We know where you are, help is arranged, here is what happens next."
7Stay engaged until it is transferred or resolved"I escalated it" is not a finish. Somebody has to say they have it.
8Document fully, then hand it overA timeline with times, names and actions. Then into the shift handoff, even if resolved.
What you do not do

You do not authorise a tow, book a replacement vehicle at the operator's expense, promise a refund, tell a passenger to take a taxi and claim it back, contact the press or a third party, or speculate to anyone about what caused it. Every one of those is a client decision, and several of them have legal consequences.

The one-breath escalation

Say it in this order

"What has happened — vehicle broken down on I-35 northbound, mile marker 412. Who is affected — Mr Okafor, one passenger, on his way to DFW for an 05:50 departure. Is anyone hurt — no. What I have done — driver is safe on the hard shoulder with hazards on, passenger is in the vehicle, I have the exact location. What I need — a recovery vehicle and a replacement car, and a decision about the flight. Time pressure — check-in closes in 90 minutes."

Lesson 3 of 4

20.3 Eight situations, worked through

Eight situations you will meet. In each one, the first move is the same — establish safety — and the rest follows the client's procedure. What follows is the shape of a correct response, not a substitute for the client's own instructions.

1 · Accident

Emergency services first, always.

Establish location and injuries. Call or confirm emergency services have been called. Then the client's emergency contact immediately. Take no statement about fault from anyone, offer no opinion, and record only what you were told and by whom. Do not contact the passenger's family or employer unless the client instructs it.

2 · Vehicle breakdown with a passenger aboard

Exact location, is the vehicle in a safe position, is anyone at risk from traffic, is the passenger comfortable and do they have a working phone. Escalate for recovery and a replacement vehicle. Tell the passenger and the arranger what is being arranged and when. If a flight is involved, say clearly whether it is still achievable so they can make their own decision.

3 · Driver unable to complete the assignment

Illness, a vehicle fault, an overrun on the previous job. Establish whether they are safe, then escalate for cover. The passenger is the priority: if the car will be materially late or is not coming, they need to know while they still have options.

4 · Passenger stranded

Where exactly, are they safe, is it night, are they alone, are they abroad, is their phone working. Escalate for a vehicle. Stay in contact — call them back on the schedule you promise, even with no news. This is the situation where an agent's steadiness matters most to the person on the other end.

5 · Potential missed pickup

Escalate while it is still "potential". A driver 40 minutes out from a pickup in 15 minutes is not yet a failure, and the dispatcher may have an option you cannot see. Waiting until it has definitely failed removes every one of those options.

6 · Driver cannot be reached

Run the reattempt sequence — calls, voicemail, text, alternative number — on a clock, then escalate. On a live trip with a passenger aboard, escalate much faster: you cannot rule out an accident, and that possibility outranks the inconvenience of an unnecessary call.

7 · Significant flight disruption

Diversion or cancellation. The booked trip no longer matches reality. Reach the arranger, establish what the passenger is actually doing, and escalate — a car in another city usually means an affiliate, which is an approval, not an agent decision.

8 · Major service failure

A group movement collapsing, a VIP left waiting, several failures on one account in a day. Escalate above the dispatcher, per the matrix. These are account-threatening events and the client's management would always rather hear it from you at the time than from their customer the next morning.

The common thread

In all eight: establish safety, gather precise facts, escalate early, keep people informed, stay on it, write it down. If you can do those six things under pressure, you can handle a situation you have never seen before — which is the real point of this module.

Lesson 4 of 4

20.4 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Emergency response

Pass mark: 4 of 5.

A driver calls to say they have been in a collision and a passenger seems hurt. What is your first action?

Safety outranks everything. Emergency services and location first; the client's contact immediately afterwards.

A driver is 40 minutes away from a pickup that is in 15 minutes. Is this an emergency?

Waiting until a failure is certain removes every option the dispatcher had. "Potential" is when escalation is worth something.

A vehicle breaks down and the passenger will miss their flight unless they get a taxi immediately. What may you do?

Committing the operator to a recovery cost is a client decision. Your job is speed, facts and honesty about the timing so the passenger can decide for themselves.

A customer is shouting about a charge on a two-month-old invoice. Is this an emergency?

Emergencies are defined by safety and irrecoverable failure, not by volume. Handle the complaint properly; do not wake the owner for it.

You have escalated a stranded passenger to the emergency contact and they have acknowledged. What next?

Acknowledgement is not transfer. The passenger is still waiting, and they are waiting on you until someone tells you otherwise.
Phase 8 · Emergency response & escalation

Escalating to senior client personnel

≡ Syllabus · Phase 8 · Module 21
≈ 15 min
≡Definition

An escalation matrix is the client's written answer to five questions: what happened, who is contacted, how, when, and what they must be told. It is provided per client and it is not negotiable.

Knowing where it is, and having read it before your shift, is the difference between escalating in thirty seconds and escalating in fifteen minutes.

»Example

"Driver unreachable, live trip" → client dispatcher, by phone, immediately, with the trip number, driver name, last known status and every attempt you made. That row exists so you never have to work it out at 03:00.

✓Key points
  • Read the matrix before your shift, not during an incident
  • Use the contact method it specifies — an email is not a phone call
  • Give the five facts in the same order every time
  • If nobody answers, work down the chain; do not stop
21.1 The escalation matrix21.2 What to hand over21.3 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 3

21.1 The escalation matrix

Every client's matrix looks roughly like this. The names, numbers and thresholds are theirs; the shape is standard. This is an example, not a live instruction — always use the client's own.

What happenedWhoHowWhen
Accident or injuryEmergency services, then the designated emergency contactPhoneImmediately, any hour
Breakdown with passenger aboardDesignated emergency contactPhoneImmediately
Passenger strandedClient dispatcher; emergency contact out of hoursPhoneImmediately
Driver unreachable, live or imminent tripClient dispatcherPhoneAfter the reattempt sequence, typically 10–15 min
Potential missed pickupClient dispatcherPhoneAs soon as identified
Same-day change you cannot authoriseClient dispatcherPhone or board noteBefore confirming to the customer
Major service failure / VIP affectedClient operations managerPhoneImmediately
Repeat failure on one accountGroundOps supervisor and client operations managerPhone and written summarySame shift
Complaint requesting a managerGroundOps supervisorWrittenSame shift
Billing dispute or refund requestClient accountingWrittenNext business day
Groups enquiry beyond thresholdGroups specialistWritten briefSame day
Anything you are unsure aboutGroundOps senior agentWhatever is fastestBefore you act

Working the chain

1Go to the row, not to a person you likeThe matrix exists so escalations are predictable. Calling the person who is nicest to you is how a decision gets made by someone without the authority to make it.
2Use the specified methodIf it says phone, phone. An email sent at 03:00 about a stranded passenger has not escalated anything.
3If there is no answer, go to the next levelDo not stop at one unanswered call. The matrix has levels precisely because people do not always answer.
4Record each attempt with its time"Called dispatcher 03:12, no answer. Called ops manager 03:15, answered."
5Keep working while you waitEscalation runs in parallel with everything you can still do yourself.
Out of hours, the bar is higher — and when it is met, you call

Nobody wants to be woken. But an operator who finds out at 08:00 that a passenger spent the night stranded will not thank the agent who decided not to disturb them. If the row says "immediately, any hour", that is not advisory.

Lesson 2 of 3

21.2 What to hand over

In plain words — Escalating well is a thirty-second speech that lets someone who has just woken up make a decision without asking you six questions. Say the same five things, in the same order, every time.

The five facts, in order

1What has happenedOne sentence, factual, no interpretation. "Driver hasn't answered for the 05:30 Fairmont pickup."
2Who is affectedPassenger name, account, trip number, and what they are trying to do. "Mr Okafor, Vertex Group, trip 15449, DFW departure at 05:50."
3Is anyone unsafeSay it even when the answer is no. It is the first thing the other person needs to stop worrying about.
4What you have already doneWith times. "Called 04:15, 04:20, 04:25, voicemail and text left, second number tried."
5What you need, and how long there is"I need a replacement driver. Spot time is in 65 minutes." End on the decision you are asking for.
Do not bury the ask

The most common escalation failure is a long, apologetic narrative that never states what is needed. The person you woke has to interrupt you to find out what the decision is. Lead with the facts, end with the ask, and stop talking.

After the call

Confirm who owns it

"So you'll arrange cover and I'll update the passenger?" Explicitly divide the work, or both of you will assume the other has it.

Write the timeline

Every time, every name, every action, on the trip record. This is what the client reads tomorrow.

Put it in the handoff

Resolved or not. The incoming shift needs to know it happened, and what was promised to whom.

What to tell the customer while an escalation runs

Honest, specific, no speculation

"I've got this with our operations team now and they're arranging a car. I'll call you back within ten minutes whether or not I have news." Then call back within ten minutes. Not "someone will be in touch shortly", which tells them nothing and commits you to nothing they can hold on to.

Lesson 3 of 3

21.3 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Escalation

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

The matrix says a stranded passenger goes to the emergency contact by phone, immediately, any hour. It is 03:00. What do you do?

"Immediately, any hour" is an instruction, not a suggestion. The client wrote that row precisely so an agent would not have to weigh it at 03:00.

You call the dispatcher about an imminent missed pickup and there is no answer. What next?

The matrix has levels because people do not always answer. Work down it; do not stall at the first unanswered call and do not step outside your authority instead.

Which is the correct opening for an escalation call?

Facts in order, safety stated, attempts listed, ask at the end. The person you woke can decide without interrogating you.

After the escalation call, what must be explicitly settled?

Unless you divide the work out loud, both of you will assume the other has the passenger — and nobody calls them.
Phase 9 · Affiliate coordination

Affiliate operations

≡ Syllabus · Phase 9 · Module 22
≈ 25 min
≡Definition

An affiliate is another transportation company. Work you send them is a farm-out; work they send you is a farm-in. It is how an operator covers cities where it has no cars.

The trip is the customer's; the car is somebody else's. Everything about coordination follows from that one fact.

»Example

Your client's customer lands in Chicago. Your client has no Chicago fleet. A partner operator sends a car — but the customer never knows that, and your client is still accountable for every minute of it.

✓Key points
  • Sending a trip sheet is not the same as having it accepted
  • Changes must reach the affiliate and be acknowledged
  • You get status by asking; there is no shared dispatch board
  • Never give an affiliate your client's retail pricing
22.1 Online bookings and f…22.2 Farm-out22.3 Coordinating with the…22.4 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 4

22.1 Online bookings and farm-ins: Accept / Reject

≡Definition

Trips that arrive from outside — website bookings, LA Net farm-ins, partner-network trips — wait in Reservations › Online & eFarm-in until someone accepts or rejects them.

»Example

ABC Limo in Chicago farms you a trip for their client landing at DFW tomorrow. It shows with status "Booked / unaccepted"; you check it and press Accept; it moves to Unassigned on Dispatch and ABC becomes the billing contact.

✓Key points
  • Not on the board until accepted (unless auto-accept is on)
  • Rates are editable before accepting
  • You choose which emails go out
  • Reject with a reason if something can't be fixed by phone
1Open the tabReservations › Online & eFarm-in. A flag on the toolbar tells you something is waiting.
2Accept / RejectLink on the left of the row opens the review pop-up.
3Check the ratesEdit the rate table if needed and press Update Rate Information.
4Choose emailsAccepted/rejected notice, standard confirmation/cancellation, both, or neither. Message text is editable per trip.
5SubmitSubmit and Close or Submit and Go to Reservation. Accepted → Unassigned on the board.

What to check before you press Accept

  1. Date, time and time zone — a farm-in from another city arrives in the sender's time; confirm it matches your dispatch time.
  2. Routing complete — real pick-up and drop-off, airport code + airline + flight number on airport legs, terminal / meet-and-greet notes.
  3. Vehicle type you actually have — and free at that time; check Dispatch for conflicts.
  4. The rate — what the affiliate is paying you (their farm-out cost) vs. your own price for the same trip; edit the rate table if it's below your minimum, or reject.
  1. Who pays — for LA Net farm-ins the sending company is the billing contact with Direct Bill; for web bookings a card or accepted payment method.
  2. Passenger contact — mobile number present so driver-on-the-way texts work (some senders redact it; then all contact goes through the affiliate).
  3. Special requests — child seats, luggage, accessibility, VIP.
  4. Then tick which emails go out and Submit. Reject with a reason if any item fails and can't be fixed by phone.

The four email choices — pick one deliberately

Both

Accept/reject notice and the standard confirmation (or cancellation). The normal choice for a clean web booking you are happy with.

Notice only

Tells the sender you took it, without sending the customer a confirmation yet — useful on a farm-in where the affiliate, not the passenger, owns the customer relationship.

Confirmation only

The customer gets their confirmation; no accept/reject notice goes back. Rare, but used when the sender does not want the extra mail.

Neither

The KB’s own tip: send nothing while you review the trip or phone the customer, then email from the reservation once everything is right.

The message is per trip

The accept/reject notification text can be edited inside this window before you submit — so you can write “accepted, but please confirm the flight number” instead of the standard wording.

Tour · The Accept / Reject window

Lesson 2 of 4

22.2 Farm-out: sending a trip to an affiliate

≡Definition

A farm-out is a trip you sell to your customer but hand to another operator (an affiliate) to drive. You pay the affiliate less than the customer pays you.

»Example

Your Dallas client needs a car in New York. You quote $220, farm it to an LA Net affiliate in NYC for $170, and watch their driver's statuses on your own board.

✓Key points
  • The affiliate must exist under Company Resources › Affiliates
  • LA Net affiliates: statuses sync both ways in real time
  • Others: trip sheet by email, statuses by phone
  • Set trip type Farm-out → affiliate → farm-out cost → Save → LA Net

When do we farm out?

Typical reasons
  1. Out of area — the pick-up is in a city where the company has no cars (the most common case).
  2. No vehicle of that type — the customer wants a coach or a stretch and the fleet has none.
  3. Fleet fully booked — a busy day, every car and driver already assigned at that time.
  4. Not worth running — a short trip far from base, or a one-way that would leave a car stranded.
  5. Keeping the customer — a corporate account travels nationwide; you farm out rather than say no and lose the account.
How the decision is made
  1. Quote the customer your price first — they never see the affiliate's price.
  2. Find an affiliate in that city (LA Net search, or a known partner); prefer LA Net / LA Black partners for real-time status updates and easier billing.
  3. Agree the farm-out cost — what you pay them — leaving a margin (companies typically aim for 10–25% below the customer price).
  4. Confirm the affiliate has the vehicle type and is happy with flight tracking / meet-and-greet needs.
  5. Send it (below), then watch for the Affiliate Reference # and the accepted status. Chase if it stays "Offered to affiliate".

How to send it

LA Net affiliate

Six steps, in this order

  1. Set trip type to Farm-out (right column).
  2. Pick the affiliate.
  3. Open the Farm-Out Costs tab in the rates section and enter what you will pay them — the Affiliate Total is all they see; your Grand Total stays private.
  4. Save. The LA Net button errors if you skip this.
  5. Click LA Net, match their vehicle type, tick Transfer affiliate rate, Complete.
  6. Check the Affiliate Reference # field: their confirmation number means it arrived. Status becomes Offered to Affiliate, then your "Affiliate Is Assigned" status once they accept.
Outside Limo Anywhere

Manual farm-out

Prerequisites: an account for them (Accounts, type Billing Contact + Affiliate, payment method Direct Bill/Invoice — for the farm-in direction) and an affiliate profile with email and "Send trip ticket by: Email".

  1. On the trip: status Farm-out Unassigned, type Farm-out, affiliate name, farm-out cost. Save.
  2. Email/Fax › Affiliate Trip Sheet to their address.
  3. They confirm by reply or phone; you update statuses yourself.

Real-time updates

Network › My Company Profile › Receive real-time updates: Yes — on both companies. Then their driver's On the way / Arrived / Dropped off update your board one-to-one via the affiliate statuses.

Choosing an affiliate

Core has no automatic routing. The affiliate search box also matches city and other profile columns; assignment priority only orders the list. Auto Farm (LA Black add-on) offers trips by region to assigned affiliates via email/SMS and escalates when nobody accepts.

Paying them

At settlement the farm-out cost flows to Payables › Pay Affiliate. Farm-ins bill the sending operator through their account (invoice or payment request).

Re-farming a partner’s trip

A trip that came in as a farm-in normally cannot be farmed out again. To allow it, go Network › Partner Network › Partners, open the partner and tick “Designate trips from partner as In-House”. Their trips then arrive as in-house work you can pass on. It only affects future trips and must be set per partner.

The two directions, side by side

Farm-out = you owe them → Payables › Pay Affiliates. Farm-in = they owe you → the sending company is a normal customer account (Billing Contact + Affiliate, Direct Bill/Invoice) and gets invoiced through Receivables.

Lesson 3 of 4

22.3 Coordinating with the affiliate after you send it

In plain words — Once a trip is farmed out you lose the two things you normally rely on: a live status feed and a driver you can call. Everything you would have read off a screen now has to be asked for, and asked for early.

The coordination sequence

1Confirm acceptanceAn emailed trip sheet is an offer. Until the affiliate confirms in writing, nobody is covering that trip. Chase acceptance the same day; do not discover on the morning that it was never picked up.
2Get the driver and vehicle detailsAsk for them the day before — driver first name, mobile, vehicle make and colour. Passengers ask, and without these you have nothing to tell them.
3Pass on every change, and get it acknowledgedA flight change, a time change, a new passenger number. Send it and require a reply. "Sent" is not "known".
4Ask for status on the dayAt the times that matter: driver dispatched, driver on location, passenger on board. Set your own reminders; nothing will prompt you.
5Document every exchangeWho you spoke to at the affiliate, when, and what they said. If the trip goes wrong this is the entire evidence base.
6Escalate affiliate silence like driver silenceAn affiliate who will not confirm an imminent trip is the same risk as an unreachable driver, and it escalates on the same clock.

Farm-in: when the work comes to you

Accept or reject promptly

The other operator is waiting to tell their customer. A trip left unanswered is a partner relationship being damaged quietly.

Read it as carefully as an own-client booking

Farm-ins arrive with someone else's assumptions built in. Check the vehicle class, the timings and the flight yourself.

Send back what they will need

Driver and vehicle details, and status updates on the day. Give the service you would want to receive.

Their customer is not your customer

Queries from the passenger go back through the originating operator unless your client says otherwise. Do not start a direct relationship.

What never crosses the line

Your client's retail pricing, their account terms, and their other customers. The affiliate is told what the trip requires and what they are being paid — not what the customer paid. Agents leak this by forwarding a confirmation instead of a trip sheet.

When an affiliate fails

Their driver is late, their car is wrong, their passenger is stranded. From the customer's point of view your client failed, so your response is the same as for an in-house failure — with one extra step.

1Work the problem with the affiliate, urgentlyThey have the car and the driver. Get them on the phone, not on email.
2Escalate to your client at the same timeThey are accountable to the customer and will want to know before the customer tells them.
3Keep the customer informed yourselfDo not relay "the affiliate says". Give them times and facts in your client's voice.
4Record it against the affiliatePer the client's procedure. Repeat affiliate failures are a commercial decision the operator needs data for.
Lesson 4 of 4

22.4 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Affiliate coordination

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

You emailed an affiliate trip sheet yesterday and have had no reply. The trip is tomorrow morning. What is the position?

Sending is not accepting. An affiliate who has not confirmed an imminent trip is the same risk as an unreachable driver.

A passenger on a farmed-out trip asks who their driver is. Where does that information come from?

There is no shared board. Anything you would normally read off a screen has to be requested from the affiliate in advance.

Which of these must never be shared with an affiliate?

The affiliate is told what the trip requires and what they are being paid. Forwarding a customer confirmation instead of a trip sheet is how retail pricing leaks.

An affiliate's driver is 30 minutes late and the passenger is calling you. What do you say?

From the customer's point of view your client failed. Relaying "the affiliate says" transfers blame and gives the passenger nothing useful.
Phase 10 · Ride settlement & accounting support

Completed ride review

≡ Syllabus · Phase 10 · Module 23
≈ 18 min
≡Definition

A trip marked Done has happened, but it is not finished. The charges on it are provisional until someone compares what was booked against what actually occurred.

That comparison is completed ride review, and it is where the operator's money is either captured or quietly lost.

»Example

Booked: airport transfer, $165. Actually: the flight landed 50 minutes late, the driver waited, there was an extra stop, and $28 of tolls. The trip is worth $240 — but only if somebody checks.

✓Key points
  • Review compares the booking against what happened
  • Wait time, stops, tolls and parking are the usual gaps
  • You identify discrepancies; you do not resolve disputes
  • Missing information is a finding, not a blocker — flag it
23.1 Incidents, done and t…23.2 The twelve checks on…23.3 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 3

23.1 Incidents, done and the close-out

Incident log

More › Incident: log a late pickup, damage, lost item or accident with free text; tick Incident Resolved when handled. Show the Incident Report column in Dispatch › Grid Setup — a red flag appears on flagged trips; edit via right-click › Detailed Edit.

Done means the status says so

Time passing completes nothing. A trip is complete when its status is mapped to Completing/Completed (or a cancelled state). Then it appears in Settle, which is where charges, driver / affiliate / agent pay are confirmed and the trip is filed.

"I can't settle it"

Four causes: status not mapped to a completing/cancelled state; already settled (see lesson 4.17); Direct Bill/Invoice needed but not set; or an unpaid balance — take the payment (PMTS) or correct the rate data. Import Reservations (Excel template, 5 pm–5 am CT only) exists for large group bookings but is legacy — use with care.
