more ▾
IncidentSettleQuote logDelete
☐ Incident resolvedSAVE
Dispatch board — Incident Report column switched on in Grid Setup
🚩15501 · Priya Nair · late pick-up — driver held at the gate
Then the close-out
Status mapped to Completed → the trip appears under SettleCan’t settle? status not mapped · already settled · Direct Bill missing · unpaid balance
Lesson 2 of 3

23.2 The twelve checks on a completed ride

Twelve checks, in order. Run them the same way every time and you will not develop blind spots.

#CheckWhat you are looking for
1Ride statusIs it actually Done? A trip still showing as dispatched or on location did not get closed by the driver and may not have happened as recorded.
2DriverDoes the driver on the trip match who actually drove it? Late swaps often do not make it back to the record, and driver pay follows this field.
3VehicleSame question. A sedan booking run in an SUV may be a chargeable upgrade or an operator absorbing a cost.
4Actual timesCompare booked pickup and drop-off against actual. Big gaps are where wait time and hourly overruns hide.
5Wait timeIs any recorded? Is it correct against the grace period — and on an airport job, measured from actual landing?
6Additional stopsStops added on the day are the single most commonly missed charge. Check the driver's report against the booked routing.
7TollsPresent, plausible, and supported by whatever the client requires as evidence.
8ParkingAirport parking on meet & greet jobs especially. Frequently incurred, frequently unrecorded.
9Other chargesChild seats, extra hours, cleaning, anything the driver reported.
10GratuityApplied per the account's rule — and not applied twice when a customer also tipped in the car.
11Fees and surchargesAirport fees, fuel surcharge, taxes. Usually automatic, occasionally missing on a manually built trip.
12Notes and documentationAnything the driver or an agent recorded that explains a variance. If a trip looks odd and nothing explains it, that is a finding.
Two directions of error, and both matter

An undercharged trip costs the operator money. An overcharged trip costs them a customer — and usually an argument, a credit note and a damaged account relationship. Review is not revenue recovery; it is making the invoice true.

What to do with what you find

A clear, supported charge

Add it per the client's procedure. Tolls with a receipt, wait time the data supports.

Missing information

Flag it and route it — usually back to dispatch or the driver. Do not invent a figure, and do not simply leave the trip.

A discrepancy you cannot explain

Document what you found and escalate. Two hours' wait on a trip whose flight landed on time needs a human explanation before it is billed.

Lesson 3 of 3

23.3 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Completed ride review

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

Which charges are most commonly missed on a completed airport trip?

Base, gratuity and tax calculate automatically. The ones incurred on the day by a driver — waiting, an unplanned stop, tolls, parking — are the ones that need a human to capture them.

A trip shows two hours of wait time, but the flight landed on schedule and the passenger was collected 20 minutes later. What do you do?

You identify discrepancies; you do not resolve them. Billing it invites a dispute; deleting it may erase a legitimate charge you do not understand yet.

Why does an overcharged trip matter as much as an undercharged one?

Accuracy in both directions. An agent who only ever adds charges is doing half the job badly.

A completed trip shows a different driver than the one on the booking. Is that a problem?

Swaps are normal; swaps that never reach the record are not. The field drives driver pay and any later investigation of the trip.
Phase 10 · Ride settlement & accounting support

Simple ride close / settle rides

≡ Syllabus · Phase 10 · Module 24
≈ 20 min
≡Definition

Settling a ride is closing it: charges final, driver pay recorded, affiliate and agent pay recorded, ready to be invoiced. After settlement the trip is an accounting record, not an operational one.

It is deliberately hard to undo, which is exactly why you only settle trips you are sure about.

»Example

Clean airport transfer, driver reported no tolls and no waiting, charges match the booking, notes are clear. Settle it. The one beside it with an unexplained $95 line and no driver report? Leave it and flag it.

✓Key points
  • Settle only straightforward, fully documented trips
  • Anything unexplained is an exception, not a judgement call
  • A settled trip is very hard to reopen — when unsure, do not
  • Work in batches, in a fixed order, at a fixed time
24.1 What settling actuall…24.2 The settlement pass24.3 What you settle, and…24.4 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 4

24.1 What settling actually does

In plain words — Settling says: "this trip is finished, the numbers are right, send it to billing." It is a statement about accuracy, and you are the one making it.

What happens when a trip is settled

1The customer charges are fixedBase, extras, tolls, wait time, gratuity, tax. This becomes what the customer is invoiced.
2Driver pay is recordedCommission, hourly or flat, per the operator's arrangement. This flows to the driver's payables.
3Affiliate cost is recordedOn farmed-out work, what your client owes the partner operator.
4Agent commission is recordedWhere a booking agent is attached and earns a percentage.
5The trip leaves the operational worldIt stops being something dispatch or an agent adjusts, and becomes something accounting maintains.
Why reversing it is painful

Once settled, a trip may already be on an invoice, in a driver's pay run, and in the month's reported revenue. Unpicking it means touching all three. That is why "I wasn't sure, so I settled it anyway" is the one thing you must never do — leaving a trip open costs an hour; settling a wrong one costs several people a day.

The three states you will meet

Ready

Done, charges match the booking or are explained, driver report present, notes clear. Settle it.

Incomplete

Something is missing — a driver report, a toll receipt, an actual drop-off time. Not an error, just not finished. Chase it and leave the trip open.

Exception

Something is present but wrong, disputed, or unexplained. Document and escalate. Never settle an exception to clear it off the list.

Lesson 2 of 4

24.2 The settlement pass

A settlement pass is a batch of completed trips worked in one sitting, in a fixed order. Doing it the same way every time is what keeps it fast and accurate.

1Pull the listGo to Settle. It has three tabs: Payments Needed (money still to capture), Ready To Settle (completed and unsettled — this is your working list) and Settled Reservations (already closed). Filter to the period the client specifies, not "whatever looks done".
2Sort out the obvious exceptions firstScan for anything with an incident note, a large unexplained variance, or a missing driver report. Set those aside before you start, so they do not interrupt your rhythm.
3Run the twelve checks on each remaining tripModule 23. Same order every time.
4Add supported chargesTolls with evidence, wait time the data supports, stops the driver reported. Per the client's procedure, with the supporting note attached.
5Settle the clean onesEach row has its own SETTLE button, and Batch Settle Selected Trips closes several at once. Only tick the ones where every check passed and nothing is outstanding — a batch is where a doubtful trip gets settled by accident.
6Write up the exceptionsOne line each: trip number, what is wrong, what you tried, what you need. This list goes to the client and into the handoff.
7Report the passHow many reviewed, how many settled, how many held and why. Clients want the shape of the day, not just the settled count.
Never settle to clear a backlog

The pressure on a settlement pass is always to finish the list. A held trip is a visible piece of work; a wrongly settled one is invisible until an invoice is disputed six weeks later. Ten settled and four held with reasons is a better shift than fourteen settled.

Documenting each decision

ActionWhat the note must say
Settled cleanReviewed against booking, no variances. (Often implicit in the settlement itself — follow the client's rule.)
Charge addedWhat, how much, on what evidence. "Tolls $28.40 per driver report and receipt attached."
Held — incompleteWhat is missing, who you asked, when. "No driver report; requested from dispatch 09:12."
Held — exceptionWhat is wrong, what you checked, who you escalated to. "2 hrs wait, flight on time; escalated to ops 09:30."
Lesson 3 of 4

24.3 What you settle, and what you escalate

Settle these yourself

  • Charges match the booking exactly
  • Variances are small, supported and explained — a documented toll, wait time the flight data supports
  • Driver report present and consistent
  • Standard account, standard rate, nothing negotiated on the day
  • No incident, no complaint, no note flagging a problem
  • In-house work with no affiliate or agent complication

Escalate these

  • Any variance you cannot explain from the record
  • Any trip with an incident or a complaint attached
  • Disputed charges, or a customer already querying it
  • Driver pay questions or a driver disputing their figure
  • Affiliate cost that does not match what was agreed
  • Anything involving a refund, a credit or a waiver
  • A rate that was agreed verbally and is not in the system
  • Group and event trips — almost always settled by a specialist
  • Anything already settled that someone wants reopened
The test

Could you explain every line on this trip, from the record alone, to a customer who queried it? If yes, settle it. If you would have to say "I think" or "probably", it is an exception.

Reporting exceptions well

The exception list is the actual output of a settlement pass. The settled trips look after themselves; the held ones need a human, and how you write them decides how quickly that human can act.

WeakUseful
"15402 — wait time looks wrong""15402 (28 Aug, IAD arrival, Vertex Group) — 2 hrs wait charged; flight UA 901 landed on schedule 14:10, POB 14:31. No driver note explaining the gap. Not settled. Need dispatch to confirm with driver."
"15418 — missing tolls""15418 (29 Aug, DFW departure) — route crosses the toll road but no tolls recorded and no driver report. Requested from dispatch 09:12, no response yet. Held."
"15427 — customer unhappy""15427 (30 Aug) — customer emailed disputing the $45 meet & greet, says it was not requested. Booking notes show it was added at booking but no source recorded. Held pending accounting."
Lesson 4 of 4

24.4 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Ride settlement

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

What is the test for whether you may settle a trip yourself?

Settling asserts the numbers are right. If explaining a line would need "I think" or "probably", it is an exception.

You are behind on a settlement pass and four trips have unexplained variances. What do you do?

A held trip is visible work. A wrongly settled trip is invisible until an invoice is disputed weeks later, by which point it is in a pay run and a revenue report too.

Why is settling hard to reverse?

Settlement is the handover from operations to accounting, and it moves several sets of numbers at once.

Which of these can you settle without escalating?

The first is a documented, explainable variance on a standard trip — exactly what "simple ride close" means. Groups and disputes both go to someone else.
Phase 10 · Ride settlement & accounting support

Accounting support

≡ Syllabus · Phase 10 · Module 25
≈ 15 min
≡Definition

Accounting support is the work between a settled trip and a paid invoice: making sure rides are complete and correctly attributed, answering routine questions, and getting everything else to the people who own it.

The boundary is sharp. You prepare and you explain. You do not adjust, credit, refund or decide.

»Example

"Why does this invoice have two trips on the 14th? We only booked one." — you can look, and tell them one is a return leg booked separately. If it turns out to be a genuine duplicate, that is accounting's to fix, not yours.

✓Key points
  • Prepare rides for billing: complete, attributed, documented
  • Explain charges from the record; never recalculate by hand
  • Every adjustment is somebody else's decision
  • Document exceptions in a form accounting can act on
25.1 Preparing rides for b…25.2 Routine accounting qu…25.3 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 3

25.1 Preparing rides for billing

Preparing a ride for billing means making sure that when accounting picks it up, there is nothing left to ask.

1Confirm it is settledUnsettled trips do not bill. A trip that has sat open for a week is usually one somebody could not explain — find out why.
2Check it is on the right accountThe most expensive quiet error in billing. A corporate trip attached to a personal record invoices nobody and ages until someone notices.
3Check the billing requirements on the accountPurchase order number, cost centre, department code, a reference the customer's AP system requires. An invoice missing a PO number is an invoice that will not be paid.
4Check the supporting documentation is attachedToll receipts, parking receipts, driver reports, anything the client requires to support a variable charge.
5Identify missing chargesA completed trip with no tolls on a route that has them, or no wait time on a flight that landed 90 minutes late, is worth a second look before it bills.
6Flag payment problemsA declined card, an expired card, an account over its terms. Route it — do not contact the customer about payment unless the client's procedure says you may.
The account is the single most important field

Everything downstream — the rate that applied, who gets invoiced, on what terms, with which reference — follows from which account the trip is attached to. A trip on the wrong account is not a small error; it is an invoice that cannot be sent.

Common findings and where they go

FindingRoute to
Trip on the wrong accountAccounting, with both account names and the trip number. Do not move it yourself unless the client permits it.
Missing PO or cost centreThe booking contact, per the client's procedure — usually a simple request.
Missing toll or parking receiptDispatch or the driver.
Declined or expired cardAccounting. Never take new card details yourself.
Duplicate tripAccounting, with both trip numbers and what you checked.
Account over termsAccounting, and flag it before taking further bookings if the client requires that.
Lesson 2 of 3

25.2 Routine accounting questions you can answer

In plain words — There is a short list of accounting questions you can answer, and everything else is a routing job. Knowing which is which keeps you fast and keeps you out of trouble.

You can answer these

  • "What is this charge?" — read the line from the trip and say what it is
  • "Which trip is this?" — date, passenger, route, confirmation number
  • "Was gratuity included?" — from the record
  • "Why are there two trips that day?" — look, and explain what you find
  • "When was this trip?" — and what was booked
  • "Has our invoice been sent?" — if the client gives you that visibility
  • "What is your cancellation policy?" — read it from the client's policy, do not paraphrase from memory

You route these

  • Any request to change, credit, waive or refund
  • Any dispute about an amount
  • Payment method changes or new card details
  • Payment terms, credit limits, account status
  • Anything about a settled trip that needs reopening
  • Driver pay questions
  • Affiliate invoices and costs
  • Tax questions
  • Anything where you would be guessing
Never take card details

Not over the phone, not by email, not "just to pass on". Payment information goes through the client's own secure process, always. This is not a matter of procedure preference — handling card data outside that process creates a real liability for everyone involved.

Writing an accounting exception

Accounting is working from your note, often days later, without the context. Give them everything in one pass.

A complete exception

"Trip 15402 — 28 Aug, Vertex Group, Mr Okafor, IAD arrival. Issue: customer (Dana Whitfield, dana.w@vertex.com, 214-555-0117) disputes 3 hrs wait time on invoice 8841. What the record shows: UA 901 landed 14:10 on schedule; POB recorded 17:05. No driver note explaining the gap. What I have done: reviewed the trip, made no changes, asked dispatch to confirm with the driver (09:12, no response yet), told Dana accounting would come back to her today. What is needed: a decision on the wait time charge and a call back to Dana."

Trip, issue, evidence, actions taken, decision needed. The same five-part shape as an escalation, because it is one.

Lesson 3 of 3

25.3 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Accounting support

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

A customer calls to update the card on their account because the old one expired. What do you do?

Card data never passes through an agent, in any channel, for any reason. It goes through the client's own secure process.

Which of these can you answer yourself?

Explaining a charge from the record is squarely yours. Removing it is a decision, and account terms are accounting's to state.

You find a completed trip attached to a personal record when the customer books under a corporate account. Why does it matter?

The account drives everything downstream. A misattributed trip prices wrong, bills nobody, and ages quietly until someone finds it.

What must an accounting exception note contain?

Accounting reads it days later with no context. Five parts, every time — the same shape as an escalation, because it is one.
Phase 11 · Shift handoff & operational continuity

Handoff from the previous agent

≡ Syllabus · Phase 11 · Module 26
≈ 18 min
≡Definition

A handoff is the written transfer of everything unfinished from one agent to the next. GroundOps runs continuous coverage across shifts and time zones; the handoff is the only thing that makes it continuous.

Its test is simple: could someone who has never seen any of this pick it up cold and get it right?

»Example

03:00. A passenger's flight was diverted and you arranged a 07:00 car through an affiliate, pending their confirmation. Your shift ends at 04:00. If that is not written down, nobody chases the confirmation and a stranded passenger stays stranded.

✓Key points
  • Read the incoming handoff before you do anything else
  • Write yours throughout the shift, not in the last five minutes
  • Six fields per item: what, status, done, next, who, when
  • An item with no owner and no deadline is not a handoff item
26.1 Starting a shift26.2 The handoff record26.3 Ending a shift26.4 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 4

26.1 Starting a shift: reading the handoff

In plain words — The first ten minutes of a shift decide the rest of it. Read the handoff, then look at the board, then answer the phone. Not the other way round.
1Read the whole handoff before acting on any of itItems interact. A driver flagged for monitoring and a late-running trip on the same account are one problem, not two.
2Sort it by when it bitesAnything affecting a ride in the next few hours first. A quote follow-up due Thursday can wait until you have breathed.
3Check anything marked waitingHas the affiliate confirmed? Did accounting come back? Did the customer send the flight number? Several will have resolved themselves overnight; the rest are yours now.
4Query anything you cannot followWhile the outgoing agent is still reachable. "What does 'Dana chasing' mean on 15449?" is a thirty-second question now and an hour's archaeology later.
5Then sweep the board yourselfThe handoff is what the last agent knew. It is not what is true. Check unassigned trips, early pickups, wake-up calls due and inbound flights independently.
6Acknowledge itPer the client's method. Somebody needs to know the handoff was received and read, not just written.
The handoff is a claim, not a fact

"Driver confirmed for the 05:30" means someone believed that at 22:00. It is worth four hours of trust and no more. On anything critical in your shift, verify it yourself — especially assignments, affiliate confirmations and anything that was "about to be sorted".

What you should find in an incoming handoff

Customer-facing

Outstanding requests, pending changes, unconfirmed reservations, open quotes, group enquiries awaiting follow-up, complaints in progress.

Operational

Drivers being monitored, wake-up calls due, late or potentially late rides, connection problems, affiliate confirmations outstanding.

Administrative

Settlement exceptions, accounting items, escalations in flight, and emails read but not yet answered.

Lesson 2 of 4

26.2 The handoff record

Each item gets six fields. Anything less and the next agent has to ask; anything more and nobody reads it.

1What happenedOne sentence, with the trip or account number. "Trip 15449 — flight diverted to BWI."
2Current statusWhere it stands right now. "Passenger at BWI, aware, waiting."
3What has already been doneWith times. "Affiliate Hudson Exec asked at 02:40 to cover 07:00 BWI → DC."
4What still needs to happenThe actual next action, not a description of the problem. "Chase Hudson for written confirmation."
5Who has been contactedNames and roles. "Dana Whitfield (arranger) told at 02:50. Ops manager Ray Santos aware, 02:45."
6By whenA real time. "Confirmation needed by 05:30 or escalate to Ray again."

A handoff item, written out

Trip 15449 — Vertex Group / Mr Okafor — diverted flight

What: UA 901 to IAD diverted to BWI, landed 02:15. Original 02:40 IAD pickup is dead.
Status: Passenger at BWI, aware, waiting airside. Comfortable, phone working.
Done: Cancelled the IAD trip 02:35. Asked Hudson Exec (affiliate, dispatch@hudsonexec.com, 410-555-0142) at 02:40 to cover 07:00 BWI → Washington DC, sedan. Told Dana Whitfield (arranger) 02:50. Escalated to Ray Santos (ops mgr) 02:45 — he approved the affiliate cost.
Next: Hudson has NOT confirmed in writing. Chase.
Who: Dana Whitfield 214-555-0117 expects an update by 06:00.
By when: Written confirmation needed by 05:30. If not received, call Hudson dispatch directly and re-escalate to Ray.

Write it as it happens

A handoff written in the last five minutes of a shift is written from memory, and memory drops the details that matter — the times, the names, the exact thing you promised someone. Keep the record open and add to it as each thing occurs.

Two rules about what goes in

Everything unfinished goes in

Including things you think will resolve themselves, and things you are slightly embarrassed about. An item you left out because "it's probably fine" is the one that fails.

Nothing finished goes in

A handoff full of completed work buries the four things that actually need attention. Finished work belongs in the trip record, not the handoff.

Lesson 3 of 4

26.3 Ending a shift: writing the handoff

In plain words — The last twenty minutes of a shift are for closing what can be closed and writing down what cannot. Not for starting anything new.
1Stop taking on new open-ended workWhere the client's staffing allows it. Something you start at 05:50 and hand over at 06:00 is worse handled than something the next agent starts fresh.
2Close what can be closedA confirmation you can send, a note you can write, a customer you can call back. Anything you can finish should not become a handoff item.
3Sweep the board one more timeUpcoming pickups, unassigned trips, wake-up calls in the next few hours, flights inbound. Catch it now rather than handing over a surprise.
4Sweep the inboxAnything read but unanswered, anything waiting on someone else. Both are handoff items.
5Complete the handoff recordSix fields per item, ordered by when each one bites, not by when it happened.
6Hand over live where you canA two-minute conversation over the top of a written handoff catches what writing misses — tone, doubt, "watch this one". Where shifts do not overlap, say so in the note: "call me if 15449 isn't confirmed."

The end-of-shift checklist

CheckAsk yourself
Rides in the next 6 hoursIs everything assigned, accepted, and does anything need a wake-up call?
Live and imminent exceptionsIs anything late, unconfirmed, or unresolved right now?
Promises I madeDid I tell anyone I would call them back? Is that written down with the time?
Waiting on someone elseAffiliates, accounting, dispatch, customers. Each one an item.
Open quotes and group enquiriesAny with a follow-up due in the next 24 hours?
Escalations in flightWho owns each one now, and what is still outstanding?
Settlement exceptionsAnything held, and what it is held for?
Anything I am uneasy aboutWrite it down even if you cannot articulate why. "Watch 15461, driver was vague" is legitimate.
The promise field is the one that gets people

"I'll call you back within ten minutes" made at 05:55 becomes the next agent's obligation at 06:05 — and they will not know about it unless you write it down. Every promise you made and did not keep goes into the handoff, by name, with the time it is due.

Lesson 4 of 4

26.4 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Shift handoff

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

The incoming handoff says "driver confirmed for the 05:30". It is now 04:00. What is the right attitude to that line?

A handoff is a claim about the past, not a fact about the present. Trust it for context; verify anything that matters in the next few hours.

Which of these belongs in a handoff?

Only unfinished work. An unkept promise is the incoming agent's obligation and they cannot honour it if they do not know about it.

What are the six fields of a handoff item?

Those six answer every question the incoming agent would otherwise have to ask — and the last two are the ones most often left off.

When should the handoff record be written?

Written at the end, it is written from memory — and memory drops exactly the details that matter: the times, the names and what you promised.

Client configuration, policies & SOPs

≡ Syllabus · Phase 12 · Module 27
≈ 45 min
≡Definition

Configuration is the set of switches that decide how the software behaves for this company: what it sells, what it drives, how it prices, who may log in.

»Example

"Why doesn't the SUV show up for airport trips?" → the SUV vehicle type isn't ticked for the From Airport service type. Five clicks in Company Resources fixes it.

✓Key points
  • Section 03 = where things are; this section = what to set
  • Rarely changed, constantly felt
  • Each lesson is one small task
  • Rates are the part people find hardest — go slowly there

Lesson 1 of 11

27.1 Company settings and preferences

In plain words — "Configuration" means the switches that decide how the software behaves for this company. Most were set when the company joined. As an agent you will rarely flip them, but you will be asked "why does it do that?" every day, and the answer is almost always one of these switches. This section teaches the ones you can safely touch and where the rest live.

Start at My Office›Company Settings. Two pages matter most:

Contact Information

Company name, address, phone and the email addresses used on outgoing paperwork. Upload a logo and it replaces the text block on confirmations — so put the phone and email on the logo itself. Never use a free Gmail/Yahoo address here: emails go out through Limo Anywhere's mail service and need the company's own domain to be trusted.

Company Preferences

Seven tabs of switches. Press Update My Company Preferences at the bottom or the change is lost. The tabs are summarised below; the Reservations tab gets its own lesson (6.9).

TabWhat lives there (the ones you'll notice)
GeneralTime zone · date & time format · currency · default state · address format · which page opens at login · default trip type (In-house / Farm-in / Farm-out) · alert for new online reservations · Master delete password · custom labels (call a passenger a "guest", a reservation a "job")
Forms & ReportsWhat customers, drivers and affiliates see on paperwork: show rates to drivers or not, itemised charges on confirmations, drop-off time on emails, signature line on trip sheets, font sizes
Greeting SignThe default three-line meet-and-greet sign, built from tags like passenger name and company
Accounts, Calendar, QuotesAccount numbers auto or manual · required account fields (the cause of "payment method is required" pop-ups) · calendar default view and week start
ReservationsPop-up vs in-page editing · autocomplete · auto-populate hours / passengers / stops / distance · read-back script · credit card required · vehicle-type vs car warning · copy and round-trip behaviour
Settle, Receivables, PayablesWhether unsettled trips can be invoiced · alert after N hours for done-but-unsettled trips · driver hours from trip duration or garage times
Driver AnywhereWhich app rate fields map to which line items · wait-time grace periods (airport vs non-airport) · when drivers must collect payment

Tour · Where company preferences live, group by group

My Office › Company Settings › Company Preferences
Lesson 2 of 11

27.2 System users: giving colleagues access

In plain words — Every person who logs in needs their own user. The company's administrator creates it; the person then gets an email to set a password. Sharing logins is not allowed — every change in the system is stamped with the user who made it.
1OpenMy Office›Company Settings›System Users › Add
2Fill inFirst and last name, mobile, email (the invite goes here), username (best practice: the same email), primary role (reporting only)
3SaveAn invite email is sent within a minute. It expires within a day — if it goes stale, use Forgot password on the login page.
4Restrict (optional)New users see everything by default. Untick modules or sub-modules they should not open.

By module

Block whole icons (My Office, Reports, Dispatch, Settle, Receivables, Payables) or parts — e.g. allow invoicing but not payments, or hide System Users so someone cannot re-enable their own access.

By schedule

A date range for temporary staff, or hours and weekdays (9–6, Mon–Fri) for shift workers.

By IP address

Allow or block specific office IP addresses so a login only works from the office.

Off-boarding

Edit the user: Activation → Inactive, Lock-out → Locked, note the reason. Never delete — history stays attached to the user.

Password rules

Back office: at least 12 characters with upper and lower case, a number and a symbol, and not containing the username. Driver Anywhere and passenger apps: at least 7 characters with the same mix. The Company ID is never emailed — the admin tells new users what it is.

27.3 Service types: what the company sells

In plain words — A service type is a product on the menu: "Airport pickup", "Hourly as directed", "Point to point", "Wedding charter". Picking one on a reservation decides how the price is worked out and which vehicles are offered. Set these up first; everything else refers to them.

Found under My Office›Company Settings›System Settings›Service Types. Each one has:

Code & name

A short code (AIRA) and an internal name (From Airport). Codes are arbitrary but permanent once used.

Custom label

What customers see on the website, e.g. "Airport departure — please book 2 hours ahead".

Pricing type

Fixed (zone to zone), Hourly, Per passenger, Distance (per mile) or Fixed-or-Distance (zone price first, per-mile if none). Pick one.

Rate matrix

Which rate sheet (Default, Summer…) this service type reads for fixed and distance prices.

Visible in ORES

Show it on the online booking widget or keep it back-office only.

Default mapping

One service type each must be marked as the company's point-to-point, airport arrival, airport departure and hourly. Quick Rate Lookup and the passenger app use this when a customer never chooses a service type.

Try the price resolver

Change the pricing type and whether a zone pair exists, and see what the customer gets.

Lesson 4 of 11

27.4 Vehicle types and the fleet

In plain words — A vehicle type is a category on the menu ("SUV", "Sedan", "Sprinter"). The fleet is the list of real cars with plate numbers. Prices are attached to the type, never to the individual car — three different SUVs under the "SUV" type all cost the customer the same.
Company Resources › Vehicle Types

Add a vehicle type

  1. Enter a unique code (SUV, SED) and a title.
  2. Choose hourly or per-passenger as its main rate style.
  3. Passenger and luggage capacity — this is what the website checks, not the car's.
  4. Colour code for the dispatch grid; description and photo for the website.
  5. Tick the service types this vehicle may be used for. Unticked = never offered for that service.
  6. Optionally hide it from online booking or mark it accessible. Save.

Never delete a vehicle type — set it Inactive, or reports and old trips break.

Company Resources › Fleet

Add a car

  1. Code (SUV-3), description, make, model, year, colour, plate.
  2. Pick its vehicle type — this is the link that makes pricing and the dispatch warning work.
  3. Capacity, status Active. Everything else (VIN, insurance, mileage) is optional.

Set up all vehicle types first, then the cars.

Drivers

Company Resources›Drivers: name, mobile and carrier (for texts), licence, then the web access username/password and the Driver Anywhere settings tab — nothing reaches the app until that first box is ticked. Pay schedules per vehicle type live here too.

Airports & airlines

All airports are pre-loaded but inactive. Show All, find yours, set Active — that puts it in the reservation dropdown. Same for airlines; private airlines (FBOs) need an address.

Points of interest

Stadiums, hotels, venues the company goes to often, with a category and address, so they can be picked from the POI tab.

27.5 Rates: how a price is built

In plain words — A price on a trip is a short list of lines: a base fare, a tip, tax, maybe a fuel fee, maybe a discount. The System Rate Manager defines those lines once for the company, and each line is told what kind of number it is and what it is calculated on. Get that right and the maths is automatic.

My Office›Rate Management has four pages: System Rate Manager (the lines), Fixed Rates & Zones (zone-to-zone prices), Special Promotion Setup (promo codes) and Miscellaneous Fees (rule-based extras). Hourly, per-passenger and distance prices are set on the vehicle type instead.

Rate type

Fixed

One dollar amount. Flat Rate, Tolls, Parking.

Rate type

Multiplier

Quantity × amount. Per Hour, Per Pass, Extra Stops, Child Seats.

Rate type

Percentage

% of a defined base. Gratuity, Tax, Surcharge.

GratuityTotal of all base ratesStd Grat 20%

Surcharge 1Base + gratuities + taxes + misc feesFuel surcharge
Surcharge 2Base + taxes + misc (excludes gratuity)STC surcharge
Discount (total)Deducted from the grand totalPromo $
Discount (base)Deducted from base before everything else calculatesCorporate 10%
MiscellaneousAdded; excluded from gratuity/taxAirport fee, late-night fee

Lesson 6 of 11

27.6 Fixed rates and zones

In plain words — "From the airport to downtown in an SUV is $165." That is a fixed rate: a set price between two zones. A zone is either an area (a city, or a group of zip codes) or an airport. Build the zones first, then the prices between them.
1Open the matrixRate Management›Fixed Rates & Zones Setup › pick the rate sheet (Default is the one customers use).
2Define zones (…)Area zone: code (SDAL), description, city or cities, state, zip codes. Airport zone: the FAA code as the zone code (DFW, DAL), city/zip blank.
3Add a rateFrom zone → to zone, vehicle type, price; optional tolls, parking, taxes. Tick Create reverse rate for the return direction.
4Bulk uploadHundreds of zones? Fill in support's spreadsheet templates (zones first, then rates — vehicle type codes must already exist).

Zip codes carve up a city

"Dallas" with no zips is one giant zone. Add zips and it shrinks to those zips — so you can make "North Dallas" and "South Dallas" with different prices.

Multiple rate sheets

Default, Summer, Event weekend… one is flagged as default; a service type or a customer account can point at a different sheet.

Fixed always wins online

If a zone pair exists, web customers see the fixed price and never the per-mile one. Back-office staff can still choose either tab.

Lesson 7 of 11

27.7 Hourly, per-passenger and distance rates

In plain words — These three are "rate × something": rate × hours, rate × passengers, rate × miles. Because the "something" comes from the trip, these prices live on the vehicle type (Company Resources › Vehicle Types › edit › Rates tab) — six clicks deep, and the place people most often can't find.

Hourly

Standard rate per hour, a minimum number of hours, optional tiers (hours 1–2 at $150, 3+ at $120) and a peak-rate schedule (one time block per weekday). Choose which multiplier line the result lands in — normally Per Hour.

Minimums are a gate, not a rounding rule: book below the minimum online and the vehicle is simply not offered.

Per passenger

Same idea: rate per passenger, minimum passengers, tiers, and a target line such as Per Pass. If that line is disabled in the System Rate Manager it won't appear as a choice — enable it first.

Distance

Per mile or km, in tiers: first 1 mi $65 · next 19 mi $0 · remaining $1.50 gives a $65 minimum that covers 20 miles. Alternatively a flat "minimum mileage charge" per sheet. Result goes into one flat-rate line or a set of multiplier lines (Company Preferences › Reservations › Auto-populate distance total — which is also the on-switch for Google address lookup).

Rates are snapshots

A reservation copies the rate table the moment it is created. Changing a rate later affects new reservations only; press Apply Rate Table again on an old one if it should be re-priced.

Stored Rates — Multiplier Rate
Per Hour — (Base Rate)Per Pass — (Base Rate)Extra Stops — (Base Rate)Per km — (Base Rate)Per Unit — (Base Rate)

A multiplier rate is a quantity × an amount. The rate itself only says which quantity to use — the amount comes from the price list.

Every one of these is "how many × how much": hours, passengers, extra stops, kilometres.

Lesson 8 of 11

27.8 Promo codes, fees and extras

Rate Management › Special Promotion Setup

Promo codes

A code the customer types online or an agent picks on the reservation. Rules limit where it works: service types, zip codes, vehicle types, airports, a date or date range. Two flavours — Is Discount ticked = a % or $ off the base rates (flat, per hour, per passenger, or tiered); unticked = a replacement rate that overrides every line. Set old codes Inactive rather than deleting so reports keep working (Sales Revenue report › filter by promo code).

Rate Management › Miscellaneous Fees

Rule-based fees

"$20 late-night fee when pickup is in Dallas, point-to-point, between 1:00 and 6:59 AM." Pick the line item it posts to, Mandatory (auto-applies online) or Optional (the back office asks), then the criteria: service types, vehicle types, airport codes, pickup/drop-off text, dates and times.

Credit-card processing fee

Two ways. Everyone pays by card → a percentage line in Surcharge 4 in the System Rate Manager (e.g. 3%, primary). Only some do → make the line with default 0 and add a Mandatory misc fee that applies on the right service/vehicle types, so ORES and the app add it automatically.

Child seats & airport meet options

Child seat: a multiplier line (default $15 × 0); the reservation's child-seat count fills the quantity when auto-populate child seats is on. Meet options: Company Preferences › Reservations › Airport Meet Option — separate prices and labels for curbside and inside ("Meet & Greet"), shown online and in the back office.

Lesson 10 of 11

27.10 The client SOP pack

In plain words — Everything in this academy so far is how the work is done in general. The client SOP pack is how it is done here, for this operator. Where the two differ, the client wins — every time, without exception.

What the pack must tell you before your first live shift

AreaWhat you need from the client
IdentityThe exact greeting, the company name as spoken, hours, time zone, and how to refer to yourself.
Services and areasWhat they sell, where they cover, and where they farm out.
FleetTheir vehicle names and what each one actually seats and carries. Their names, not the generic ladder.
RatesWhich rate tables apply, what is included in a quoted price, and what you may and may not quote.
PhoneGreeting, hold and transfer rules, what may be disclosed and to whom, how to document.
EmailWhich inboxes, how to claim, response-time targets, signature block.
ReservationsRequired fields beyond the system minimum, confirmation process, who receives what.
QuotesValidity period, follow-up schedule, what you may quote without approval.
Groups & eventsThe threshold at which you hand over, and to whom.
Cancellation & no-showThe exact windows and charges. Never from memory.
AirportClearance allowances domestic and international, grace periods, meet & greet policy and fee, pickup zones.
DispatchWhat you may do on the board and what you may not. The light-dispatch boundary, in their words.
Driver monitoringWhen and how you may contact a driver, and what you may tell a passenger about them.
Wake-up callsWhich drivers, how far ahead, reattempt intervals, escalation point.
AffiliatesWho they use, how work is sent, what must be confirmed, what must never be shared.
EmergencyThe procedure, and the named contacts with numbers, for every hour of the day.
Accounting & settlementWhat you may settle, what evidence is required, where exceptions go.
Escalation matrixThe full table: what, who, how, when, what information.
After hoursWhat changes outside the client's office hours, and who is on call.
HandoffThe format, where it lives, and how it is acknowledged.
If a row is blank, that is a finding

A client SOP pack with no escalation matrix, or no cancellation windows, or no named emergency contact is not ready to be worked. Raise it before your first shift, not at 03:00 on the night it matters. "It wasn't in the pack" is not an acceptable explanation for a stranded passenger.

How to use the configuration lessons in this module

The nine lessons before this one show you where the client's configuration lives in Limo Anywhere — their company settings, their service types, their vehicles, their rate structure. Read them alongside the SOP pack: the pack tells you the policy, and the configuration shows you how that policy is expressed in the system you will be working in. When a customer says "it priced differently last time", the answer is almost always in one of those nine screens.

Lesson 11 of 11

27.11 Knowledge check

Knowledge check 06

Configuration

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

A trip's gratuity is calculating on top of the state tax. What is wrong?

Gratuity calculates on the total of the Base group; a "tax" placed in Base will be tipped on. The group, not the name, drives the math.

You lowered the SUV hourly rate from $150 to $120. A reservation created last week still shows $150. Why?

Rate changes only affect new reservations; existing ones keep their snapshot unless you re-apply the rate table.

Addresses save without any Google verification and no mileage is ever calculated. Which preference is off?

Despite its name, that setting is the switch for Google lookup and distance pricing.

To make a fixed rate from Dallas Love Field to downtown, the airport zone's code must be…

Airport zones match on the FAA code; area zones match on city/state/zip.
Phase 13 · End-to-end scenario training

Real-world operational scenarios

≡ Syllabus · Phase 13 · Module 28
≈ 40 min
≡Definition

A scenario is a situation with no module label attached. Real calls do not announce which chapter they belong to, and most of them need two or three at once.

These twenty-one are the situations GroundOps agents actually meet. Work them before you meet them live.

»Example

"Our driver never turned up and my colleague had to get a taxi — and while I've got you, can you move Friday to the 10th?" That is a complaint, a service failure, an accounting exception and a reservation change in one breath.

✓Key points
  • Identify what kind of situation it is before you act
  • Safety, then irrecoverability, then everything else
  • Most scenarios need more than one module
  • Say what you did and why — the reasoning is what is being assessed

Lesson 1 of 5

28.1 How to work a scenario

Work each scenario out loud or on paper before reading the notes. What matters is not arriving at the same answer as the notes, but being able to say why you did what you did.

The four questions, in order

1Is anyone unsafe?If yes, that is the whole answer until it is resolved. Everything else waits.
2Is something about to fail irrecoverably?A flight, a meeting, a wedding. If yes, this is an emergency and the clock is the constraint.
3What am I authorised to do here?Do that part immediately. Everything beyond it is an escalation, started in parallel.
4Who needs to know, and by when?Passenger, arranger, driver, dispatch, client, next shift. Usually more than one.

How you will be assessed on these

What is being looked for

  • Correct identification of the situation
  • Safety and urgency judged correctly
  • Acting within your authority, and recognising where it ends
  • Communication to the right people in the right order
  • A record someone else could pick up

What fails a scenario

  • Promising something you cannot authorise
  • Waiting for certainty before escalating
  • Solving it and telling nobody
  • Explaining a cause you cannot verify
  • Leaving it undocumented
There is rarely one right answer, but there are wrong ones

Two competent agents will handle a diverted flight slightly differently and both be correct. Neither of them will have offered the customer a refund, told the passenger to take a taxi and claim it back, or gone off shift without writing it down.

Lesson 2 of 5

28.2 Scenarios 1-7: the customer reaches you

Seven scenarios where the customer initiates. The modules in brackets are where the material lives.

1 · A new reservation call

A caller you do not recognise wants a car for Thursday. Work it: greeting, identify the caller, search three ways before creating anything, establish it is a new booking, gather the fifteen fields, read back with the weekday, give the confirmation number, document. Watch for: creating a duplicate account; missing the mobile number. (M4, M7, M11, M12)

2 · A reservation request by email

Four facts, eight gaps. Work it: claim it, check against the fifteen fields, reply once with all the questions numbered and a deadline, set the follow-up. Watch for: asking one question at a time; booking on guesses. (M5, M7)

3 · A quote request

"What would four of us cost from the Ritz to JFK on the 22nd?" Work it: gather as though booking, price from the system, offer two classes with the capacity noted, state what is included, give a validity date, say what you need to book it, record it and set the follow-up. Watch for: quoting a number you cannot find in the system; forgetting the follow-up. (M9, M14)

4 · A Groups & Events enquiry

Forty delegates, four days. Work it: recognise immediately that this is past your line, gather the full event brief anyway, hand over with the movement schedule and contacts, tell the customer who will contact them and when. Watch for: giving a ballpark figure on the way out; multiplying a sedan rate. (M15)

5 · A last-minute reservation

A car needed in two hours, rush hour, for a flight. Work it: six essentials fast, do not quote a time, check availability and drive time with dispatch, come back with a real answer including whether the flight is achievable, confirm the price, document. Watch for: "about half an hour" said to be helpful. (M13)

6 · A last-minute change

At 22:00, move tomorrow's 08:00 to 06:00. Driver assigned. Work it: buy yourself the check — "let me make sure we can cover that" — run the seven impact checks, confirm with dispatch, then confirm to the customer, then actively notify the driver, then document. Watch for: saving the change and assuming the driver knows. (M13)

7 · A message for someone else

A caller wants the accounts manager, who is asleep. Work it: six fields — who, contact, subject with the invoice number, what they want, by when, what you have already done — judge the urgency honestly, route it, tell the caller what you have done, document, handoff if unresolved. Watch for: omitting what you already did. (M6)

Lesson 3 of 5

28.3 Scenarios 8-14: the day goes wrong

Seven scenarios where the day goes wrong. These are the ones that separate a trained agent from an untrained one.

8 · A flight is delayed

Two hours late, driver already dispatched. Work it: verify from the flight data, confirm the pickup has moved with the flight, tell dispatch and the driver, tell the arranger, check the driver's next job is not now in conflict, document. Watch for: assuming monitoring told the driver; ignoring the knock-on trip. (M8, M17, M19)

9 · A flight is diverted

Landed in a different city. Work it: the booked trip is dead. Reach the arranger, establish what the passenger is actually doing, escalate — a car in another city is an affiliate decision and a cost approval. Keep the passenger informed on a schedule you promise and keep. Document a timeline. Watch for: cancelling unilaterally; waiting for the customer to call you. (M8, M20, M22)

10 · The driver is running late

Position says they will miss the spot time by fifteen minutes. Work it: do the arithmetic before anyone asks, tell dispatch, call the passenger with a real ETA, ask whether it still works for them — that answer decides whether this is a delay or an emergency — call back when you said you would, document. Watch for: waiting for the passenger to call; explaining the cause. (M17, M20)

11 · The passenger cannot find the driver

Status says Arrived; the passenger says there is no car. Work it: this is a connection problem, not a lateness problem. Establish exactly where each of them is — terminal, level, door. Give each the other's location in plain words. Connect them per the client's rule. Stay on it until they are together. Escalate if it runs past ten minutes or the passenger is vulnerable. Watch for: closing it on "they should find each other now". (M8, M17, M20)

12 · A wake-up call goes unanswered

Three attempts, voicemail, text, second number. Work it: escalate on the clock, not on a feeling. One-breath escalation: who, which job, what the consequence is, what you tried, how long there is. Keep trying in parallel. Follow the outcome through to the reservation and the passenger. Document every attempt with times. Watch for: redialling for fifteen minutes. (M18, M21)

13 · A vehicle breaks down with a passenger aboard

02:40, interstate, 25 miles from the airport. Work it: is anyone hurt, is the vehicle safe, exact location. Emergency services if needed. Escalate immediately for recovery and a replacement. Tell the passenger and the arranger what is being arranged. Say honestly whether the flight is achievable. Stay with it. Full timeline. Watch for: authorising a tow or a taxi yourself. (M20, M21)

14 · An affiliate has not confirmed

Trip sheet sent yesterday, trip is tomorrow, silence. Work it: treat it as you would an unreachable driver. Phone, not email. Escalate on the same clock. Have a fallback discussion with dispatch before it becomes urgent. Document every contact attempt. Watch for: treating "sent" as "covered". (M22, M21)

Lesson 4 of 5

28.4 Scenarios 15-21: closing the loop

Seven scenarios about closing the loop — the work that happens after the ride, and the work that makes the next shift possible.

15 · Tracking a driver for an anxious customer

An arranger calls twice in ten minutes about a VIP pickup. Work it: read status and position together, translate into times and places rather than status words, give a real ETA, say what you are doing, offer a proactive call at a stated time rather than waiting for the third call. Note on the account that this arranger wants active updates. Watch for: saying "Unassigned" out loud. (M17, M11)

16 · A customer complaint

"Twenty-five minutes late, my CEO missed a meeting, and it's the second time." Work it: listen without defending, acknowledge the experience not the cause, record the facts and the trip number, note the repetition explicitly, route per the matrix, tell the customer exactly what you have done, offer the one thing you can actually do. Document. Watch for: explaining the cause; offering compensation. (M5, M6, M21)

17 · An escalation to senior management

A second failure on the same account in a day. Work it: this goes above the dispatcher. Five facts in order — what happened, who is affected, is anyone unsafe, what you have done, what you need and by when. Settle explicitly who owns which part. Write the timeline. Handoff even if resolved. Watch for: a long apologetic preamble that buries the ask. (M21)

18 · Reviewing a completed ride

Airport transfer, flight landed 50 minutes late, driver reported an extra stop. Work it: the twelve checks in order. Wait time from actual landing plus grace, not from the scheduled pickup. Extra stop against the booked routing. Tolls and parking present and supported. Add what is supported, flag what is missing, escalate what is unexplained. Watch for: only ever adding charges. (M23)

19 · A simple ride settlement

Fourteen completed trips, four with variances. Work it: pull the list, set aside the obvious exceptions first, run the checks on the rest, add supported charges with evidence, settle only the clean ones, write up each exception with trip, issue, evidence, actions and what is needed. Report the shape of the pass. Watch for: settling to clear the list. (M24)

20 · An accounting exception

A customer disputes three hours of wait time on a flight that landed on schedule. Work it: look, do not adjust. Read the record: landing time, POB time, driver notes. Write the five-part exception. Tell the customer honestly what you have done and who will come back to them. Never recalculate by hand and never take card details. Watch for: quoting the customer a corrected figure. (M25)

21 · A shift handoff

End of an overnight shift with a diverted flight half-resolved and two promises outstanding. Work it: stop taking new open-ended work, close what can be closed, sweep board and inbox, write six fields per item ordered by when each bites, include every promise you made with its due time, hand over live if shifts overlap. Watch for: writing it from memory in the last five minutes; leaving out the item you think will sort itself. (M26)

Work these against your client's SOP pack

Every one of these scenarios has a client-specific answer sitting behind the general one — which contact, which threshold, which wording, which charge. Run through all twenty-one with the client's pack open beside you before your first live shift, and the first time you meet one for real it will be the second time.

Lesson 5 of 5

28.5 Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Scenarios

Pass mark: 4 of 5.

What are the four questions to ask of any scenario, in order?

Safety, then irrecoverability, then authority, then communication. That order holds for every situation, including ones you have never seen.

A passenger says the driver never arrived and they took a taxi, then asks you to move a booking next week. How many things is this?

Real calls carry several situations at once. Handling the easy one and losing the rest is the classic failure.

Status reads Arrived; the passenger says there is no car. What kind of problem is this?

Most of these are two people in the same building on different levels. The fix is locations, not ETAs.

Which of these would fail a scenario assessment even if the outcome was fine?

An undocumented resolution is invisible to the next shift, the dispatcher and the client. Over-escalating occasionally is a cheap error; no record is not.

A group enquiry comes in and you are confident you could price it yourself. What do you do?

Confidence is not authority. A figure you mention becomes a number the customer holds the operator to, and the specialist then has to contradict you.
Phase 14 · Testing & certification

Testing & certification

≡ Syllabus · Phase 14 · Phase 14
≈ 30 min
≡Definition

Certification is the point at which GroundOps states that an agent can work a client's account within their assigned responsibilities. It is a judgement about competence, made against seven assessments.

The knowledge checks in this academy are a prerequisite, not the assessment. They test whether you know; the assessments test whether you can do.

»Example

An agent who scores full marks on every check but cannot take a live reservation call without losing control of it is not certified. The reverse also happens, and is also not certified.

✓Key points
  • Seven assessments, covering knowledge and practice
  • Assessed against the client's procedures, not generic ones
  • Escalation and handoff are assessed separately, and deliberately so
  • Certification is per client, not once for a career
1 The seven assessments2 What a pass looks like3 Final knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 3

The seven assessments

#AssessmentWhat is testedHow
1Industry & product knowledgeTerminology, service types, vehicle classes and capacities, airport procedures, reservation requirements, rate models, cancellation and no-show policy.Written, against the client's own policies. Modules 1–3, 7–9.
2Limo Anywhere practicalCompleting the transactions the role requires, unaided: find an account, build a reservation, apply a rate, add a driver and vehicle, modify, cancel, quote, send a confirmation, read the dispatch board.Observed, in the system. Modules 10–12, 16, 19.
3Customer communicationMock calls and written scenarios: greeting, identification, call control, disclosure boundaries, read-back, closing, documentation. Email structure and tone.Role-play plus written responses. Modules 4–6.
4OperationalLight dispatch judgement, driver tracking, wake-up calls, affiliate coordination, last-minute changes, and knowing where the boundary is.Scenario-based. Modules 13, 17–19, 22.
5AccountingCompleted ride review against a set of trips with deliberate errors; simple settlement; recognising what must not be settled.Practical exercise. Modules 23–25.
6EscalationRecognising an exception, choosing the right contact from the matrix, and delivering the five facts in order under time pressure.Live scenario. Modules 20–21.
7Shift handoffReading an incoming handoff and acting on it correctly; producing a complete outgoing handoff from a worked shift.Practical exercise. Module 26.
Why escalation and handoff get their own assessments

They are the two things an agent can appear competent without. An agent who books beautifully but does not escalate strands a passenger once a quarter; one who does not hand over properly loses somebody else's work every shift. Both failures are invisible in day-to-day observation, which is why they are tested deliberately.

Lesson 2 of 3

What a pass looks like

In plain words — Each client sets the pass mark. What follows is the standard GroundOps shape, and the kind of thing an assessor is actually watching for.

The standard

Knowledge assessments

A numeric pass mark, typically 80–85%, with certain items treated as mandatory — getting them wrong fails the assessment regardless of the total. Mandatory items are usually the safety and disclosure ones: what you may tell a caller, when you escalate, what you may never authorise.

Practical assessments

Not scored as a percentage. The agent completes the task unaided, correctly, and can explain their reasoning. An assessor who has to prompt has seen a fail, however pleasant the call was.

What an assessor is watching for

Passing looks likeFailing looks like
Runs the six stages of a call in order without thinking about itWanders; takes information in the order the caller volunteers it
Searches three ways before creating an accountCreates a duplicate
Reads back date with weekday, time with am/pm, flight digit by digitReads back nothing, or reads back the conversation
Says "let me check and come straight back" instead of guessingPromises availability, a price or a time they have not verified
Escalates early, with the five facts in orderWaits for certainty; buries the ask in an apology
Declines to waive, refund or authorise, and routes itOffers something to make the caller happy
Documents before the next callIntends to write it up later
Holds a trip they cannot explainSettles it to clear the list
Certification is per client

An agent certified on one account is not automatically certified on another. The industry knowledge transfers; the SOP pack, the escalation matrix, the fleet, the rates and the greeting do not. Phase 12 has to be repeated for every client, and assessments 1, 4, 6 and 7 with it.

If an assessment is not passed

1The specific gap is identifiedNot "needs more practice" — "does not consistently verify the account before disclosing booking details".
2Targeted retrainingThe modules that cover the gap, reworked, not the whole programme repeated.
3Reassessment on that assessment onlyPassed assessments stand.
4Nesting continues in the meantime where it is safeAn agent can shadow and take supervised work in areas they have passed.
Lesson 3 of 3

Final knowledge check

Knowledge check

Testing and certification

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

An agent scores 100% on every knowledge check in this academy. Are they certified?

The checks test whether you know. The assessments test whether you can do it live, against the client's procedures, unaided.

Why do escalation and shift handoff have assessments of their own?

An agent who never escalates looks fine until the night it matters. One who hands over poorly loses other people's work every shift. Neither shows up in ordinary supervision.

An agent passes a knowledge assessment with 88% but answers a disclosure question wrong. What happens?

Safety and disclosure items are mandatory precisely because an average of "mostly right" is not an acceptable standard for telling a stranger where someone is travelling.

A certified agent is moved to a second client account. What has to be repeated?

Industry and software knowledge transfer. The SOP pack, escalation matrix, fleet, rates and greeting do not, and neither do the assessments that test them.
Phase 15 · Nesting & production readiness

Nesting & production readiness

≡ Syllabus · Phase 15 · Phase 15
≈ 15 min
≡Definition

Nesting is the supervised bridge between passing the assessments and working alone. An agent moves through six steps, each one handing over a little more responsibility.

It exists because competence in an assessment and competence at 03:00 on a live account are not the same thing, and the gap between them is where customers get hurt.

»Example

A new agent takes their first live call with a senior agent listening. It goes fine. The second one is a diverted flight at 02:00 — and the value of nesting is that somebody experienced is sitting there when it happens.

✓Key points
  • Six steps: shadow, reverse shadow, supervised, QA review, certification, full production
  • Progression is a judgement, not a number of shifts
  • QA reviews thirteen things, not just call quality
  • An agent can move back a step; that is the system working
1 The six steps to full…2 What QA is looking at3 Knowledge check
Lesson 1 of 3

The six steps to full production

1ShadowingThe new agent listens while an experienced agent works. They see the six stages of a call run properly, watch the documentation being written, and hear what a real escalation sounds like. No customer contact.
2Reverse shadowingThe new agent works; the experienced agent listens and can take over at any moment. Every call is debriefed. This is where habits are corrected while they are still cheap to correct.
3Supervised productionThe agent works their own shift with a senior agent available and reviewing their work in near real time. Escalation thresholds are deliberately lower — ask early, ask often.
4QA reviewA structured review of a sample of the agent's actual work across all thirteen QA dimensions. Not a spot check: a deliberate look at calls, emails, reservations, documentation and handoffs.
5CertificationGroundOps states the agent can work this account within their assigned responsibilities. Recorded, per client.
6Full productionIndependent work, with ongoing QA at the client's agreed cadence. Certification is a start, not a finish.
Progression is a judgement, not a count of shifts

Nobody moves from reverse shadowing to supervised production because a fortnight has passed. They move because the person supervising them believes they are ready. An agent held back a week is a normal, healthy outcome; an agent advanced on the calendar is how an account gets damaged.

Moving back a step

It happens, and it is not a failure of the programme — it is the programme working. An agent who starts missing documentation, or who escalated something badly, goes back to supervised production until it is solid again. Said plainly and without drama, this is much easier to accept than most people expect.

The overnight problem

Nest people on the shift they will actually work

An agent nested entirely on day shifts, with a full client office available and mostly routine bookings, has not been prepared for the job. Overnight work is different in kind: more exceptions, fewer people to ask, higher stakes on every decision. If an agent is going to work nights, a meaningful part of their nesting has to be at night.

Lesson 2 of 3

What QA is looking at

GroundOps QA reviews thirteen dimensions. A high call-quality score with poor documentation is not a pass — the point is the whole job, not the audible part of it.

1 · Call quality

Greeting, identification, control, listening, disclosure boundaries, read-back, closing, tone.

2 · Email quality

Answer first, scannable detail, numbered questions, what happens next, no internal language, no unauthorised promises.

3 · Reservation accuracy

All fifteen fields where applicable, right account, right service type, flight linked, contact verified.

4 · Limo Anywhere proficiency

Speed and correctness in the system. Does the agent find things, or hunt for them?

5 · Quote accuracy

Priced from the system, inclusions stated, validity given, recorded, followed up.

6 · Dispatch procedures

Board worked regularly, exceptions spotted early, the light-dispatch boundary respected.

7 · Driver monitoring

Lateness identified before the customer calls; wake-up calls made on time and completed properly.

8 · Affiliate coordination

Acceptance confirmed, details obtained in advance, changes acknowledged, status chased.

9 · Ride settlement accuracy

Checks run in order, supported charges added, exceptions held and written up usefully.

10 · Documentation

Written at the time, on the right record, complete enough for a stranger to act on.

11 · Escalation

Recognised, routed correctly, five facts in order, ownership settled, followed through.

12 · Shift handoff

Incoming read and acted on; outgoing complete, current and ordered by urgency.

13 · Overall customer experience

The judgement that ties the rest together: would this customer come back, and would the client be comfortable hearing this call?

The two dimensions that predict everything else

Documentation and escalation. An agent strong in both is usually strong overall and, more importantly, is recoverable when they do get something wrong — because the record exists and the right people were told. An agent weak in both can look excellent for weeks and then produce a failure nobody can reconstruct.

Lesson 3 of 3

Knowledge check

Knowledge check

Nesting and production readiness

Pass mark: 3 of 4.

What is the difference between shadowing and reverse shadowing?

The work swaps hands. Reverse shadowing is where habits get corrected while correcting them is still cheap.

An agent has been in reverse shadowing for the agreed two weeks but is still losing control of complex calls. What should happen?

Advancing on the calendar is how accounts get damaged. Holding someone an extra week is a normal outcome, not a failure.

An agent will work overnight shifts. What does that mean for nesting?

Day-shift nesting with a full client office available does not prepare anyone for a diverted flight at 02:00 with nobody awake.

Which two QA dimensions best predict overall performance?

They also determine whether a mistake is recoverable. An agent strong in both leaves a record and tells the right people; one weak in both produces failures nobody can reconstruct.
Programme outcome

What a certified GroundOps agent can do

Upon certification, and within the responsibilities assigned by the individual client, an agent should be capable of the following.

Communicate

Answer customer calls, respond to customer emails, take and route messages, and maintain professional written and spoken communication under the client’s standards.

Book

Create and modify reservations, handle last-minute requests and changes, prepare and send quotes, and assist with Groups & Event quote requests.

Operate

Provide Light Dispatch support, track drivers, perform driver wake-up calls, and coordinate with affiliates on farmed work.

Escalate

Respond appropriately to operational emergencies and route issues to the designated senior person, rather than making unauthorised decisions.

Close out

Review completed rides, perform simple ride settlements and closeout, and provide routine accounting support.

Hand over

Receive and prepare shift handoffs so that outstanding customer and operational issues are never lost between shifts.

All knowledge checks passed.

Certification also requires the seven assessments in Phase 14 and the nesting sequence in Phase 15, both of which are observed by GroundOps QA rather than scored in this browser.
